item.dc:creator: Matt Levy

item.content:encoded:
Ladies and gentlemen, we’ve got ourselves a rematch.
Just like last year, Shohei Ohtani’s Los Angeles Dodgers and Christian Yelich’s Milwaukee Brewers are meeting in the NLCS.
And, once again, Pat Murphy’s club has home-field advantage. Games 1, 2, 6 and 7 will be at American Family Field in Milwaukee, WI.
Not everything about this Series is the same, though.
“I think it is different this year. … We’re going in to beat them,” Murphy told Fox Sports, referring to his team getting swept in 2025. “We earned it in the regular season to get home-field advantage. We’re going in to beat them, we don’t care who they have.”
If you’d like to be there to see if the Brew Crew really have what it takes to dethrone the defending World Series champion Dodgers, tickets are available for all four hypothetical contests in the Cream City.
At the time of publication, the lowest price we could find on seats for any one game in Milwaukee was $224 including fees on Vivid Seats.
Prices start at $144 including fees for fans hoping to attend a showdown at Dodger Stadium.
Ahead of the NLCS, Milwaukee battled with San Diego in a tense, back-and-forth four-game NLDS that saw instantly iconic moments like a clutch Jackson Chourio catch in Game 1, a Jackson Chourio walk-off single in Game 2 and Garrett Mitchell robbing Manny Machado of a home run in Game 4.
As for the Dodgers, the club continued their winning ways in the postseason [Editor’s Note: They haven’t lost a playoff series since the Diamondbacks beat them in the 2023 NLDS] and beat up on the formidable Braves.
Kiké Hernández smashed a home run — the 17th postseason dinger of his career, putting him ahead of Babe Ruth (!) on the all-time list — in the decisive fourth game and stellar offensive performances from Andy Pages and Max Muncy.
We can’t wait to see what comes next.
For more information, our team has everything you need to know and more about the Dodgers vs. Brewers 2026 NLCS below.
What do the cheapest tickets cost for NLCS games in Milwaukee?
A complete breakdown of all the best prices on tickets for every hypothetical game at Milwaukee’s American Family Field can be found here:
| Brewers home game dates | Ticket prices start at |
|---|---|
| Game 1 Sunday, Oct. 11 | $236 (including fees) |
| Game 2 Monday, Oct. 12 | $224 (including fees) |
| Game 6 Sunday, Oct. 18 | $235 (including fees) |
| Game 7 Monday, Oct. 19 | $277 (including fees) |
How much are the cheapest tickets for NLCS games in Los Angeles?
All of the cheapest potential Dodgers NLCS home game ticket prices are listed below.
| Dodgers home game dates | Ticket prices start at |
|---|---|
| Game 3 Wednesday, Oct. 14 | $160 (including fees) |
| Game 4 Thursday, Oct. 15 | $150 (including fees) |
| Game 5 Friday, Oct. 16 | $144 (including fees) |
How can I watch the Dodgers vs. Brewers 2026 NLCS?
For fans who prefer to watch on the tube, you can catch this nervy series on FOX and FS1.
Both providers listed above can be found on the one-stop shop known as DIRECTV.
Huge 2026-27 concerts
Fans hoping to get a concert or three in this year too are in luck.
After a bit of digging, we found that many of the biggest names in music will be on the road this year and next.
Here are just five of the biggest acts and artists we can’t wait to see live in the near future.
• RUSH
Who else is out and about? Take a look at this list of all the biggest rockers on tour in 2026 to find the show for you.
This article was written by Matt Levy, New York Post live events reporter. Levy stays up-to-date on all the latest tour announcements from your favorite musical artists and comedians, as well as Broadway openings, sporting events and more live shows – and finds great ticket prices online. Since he started his tenure at the Post in 2022, Levy has reviewed a Bruce Springsteen concert and interviewed Melissa Villaseñor of SNL fame, to name a few. Please note that deals can expire, and all prices are subject to change.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers will have time to reset rotation, bullpen, and struggling Shohei Ohtani for NLCS
item.dc:creator: Associated Press
item.description: ATLANTA — Finishing off the Atlanta Braves in four games in the NL Division Series meant more to the Los Angeles Dodgers than avoiding a winner-take-all Game 5. item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA — Finishing off the Atlanta Braves in four games in the NL Division Series meant more to the Los Angeles Dodgers than avoiding a winner-take-all Game 5.
By ending the series with a 4-1 victory, the Dodgers will have extra time to reset their rotation, bullpen and struggling slugger Shohei Ohtani for the Championship Series opening game.
"It's important. It was very important," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. "Once you get to an elimination game, a Game 5 or a Game 7, anything can happen. And to be able to win today, get back, reset, have a day off tomorrow, set the rotation, it's huge."
The extra rest means Tarik Skubal likely will be the choice to start against Milwaukee instead of handling a Game 5 against the Braves. Similarly, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow will be well rested for their expected NLCS starts.
Infielder Miguel Rojas may need the extra rest for a sore lower back that kept him out.
Also, Edwin Díaz will have ample time to reset after recording saves on back-to-back days to close out the series against Atlanta. The ninth-inning work showed Díaz is re-established as the closer.
"The team trusts me," Díaz said. "I think that was the most important thing for me, the team trusts me. They give me the ball every single day. And the last two nights it's been amazing. That's why I came here to win games and close games like this one. So I'm really happy right now."
Despite those advantages, Roberts is preparing for a tough NLCS as the Dodgers try to move closer to their goal of becoming the first NL team to win three consecutive World Series.
"We've got our work cut out," Roberts said, adding extra rest also will be important for such players as Ohtani and Freddie Freeman.
Ohtani was 2 for 13 against Atlanta and hasn't homered since Aug. 18 while dealing with injuries to his right biceps, left knee and neck that have also kept the two-way player off the mound.
"So kind of enjoy this one, get Shohei a couple of days to get back," Roberts said. "Freddie, he had a big series, but, again a couple of days will help him. Give our guys in the 'pen a little reset. So we'll be ready to go Game 1."
Díaz pitched a perfect ninth inning in the clinching win. The on-field celebration was a low-key affair, but Roberts and his players, wearing "Take October" T-shirts and goggles to protect their eyes, soon were drenched with champagne.
The Dodgers made the most of their opportunity to celebrate another postseason series win while maintaining their focus on a third straight World Series championship.
"Our goal is to win the World Series, not this series," Díaz said. "We've got eight more wins to go. So our goal is win those eight games. And at the end of the day when we win those eight games, we celebrate.
"Now we're going back to LA to keep working. I know all the guys are on the same track. Now we just celebrate a little bit, go back to LA, get working and be ready for Sunday."
Andy Pages' bases-loaded single in the seventh drove in two runs to give the Dodgers a 3-1 lead. Max Muncy added to the lead with a homer in the ninth, his third blast of the postseason.
"Obviously, we have big teams, big series coming up," Pages said. "We're going to face tough teams, so prepare for those moments, but also take advantage of the opportunity of being here and enjoying these moments. And knowing that our ultimate goal is to win the World Series. So focus on that."

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Commentary: He finally did it! Dodgers' Andy Pages ends two-year postseason slump at the perfect time
item.dc:creator: Bill Plaschke

item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
He pounded his chest twice as he left the batter’s box, and all of Dodgers nation rocked to the beat.
Andy Pages did it. He finally did it. He finally broke out of his baffling two-year October slump with a hit so powerful, he didn’t even have to climb over Kiké Hernández to get it.
How powerful? With one smooth swing he broke a tie by scoring two runs while sending two teams packing, the Atlanta Braves trudging home for the winter and the Dodgers charging into the National League Championship Series.
Yeah, it was a blast, both figuratively and literally, Pages’ two-out, two-strike bases-loaded single in the seventh inning Wednesday night silencing the lame tomahawk-chopping fans at Truist Park and giving the Dodgers an eventual clinching 4-1 victory against the Braves in the National League Division Series.
Certainly, it only gets tougher from here. In winning this best-of-five series three games to one, the Dodgers can now prepare for a best-of-seven showdown task against either the mighty Milwaukee Brewers or blazing San Diego Padres.
Yes, they will need to hit better, they will need Blake Snell to find his focus, they will need Shohei Ohtani to show up.
But…Andy Pages! Seriously! If a guy who was seven for 66 in the last two postseasons and was so helpless last year he was benched for the last three games of the World Series…if that guy can drive in the winning run from the bottom of the order? The once-fallible Dodgers may just be unbeatable.
“There’s no more talented team than the Los Angeles Dodgers,” manager Dave Roberts shouted in the postgame clubhouse. “We’re the best organization in sports, top to bottom. We’re smarter, we’re better, and we’re tougher.”
At that point, someone referenced a recent comment from Padres owner José E. Feliciano insinuating that the Dodgers, baseball’s oldest team, was composed of dinosaurs.
“And we’re dinosaurs!” shouted a voice above the clubhouse din.
If they’re dinosaurs, their first initial is “T” and their last name is ‘Rex.”
It’s OK to start seriously thinking about a three-peat now. They’re now just eight wins away but, given how mediocre the American League playoff teams appear, they could realistically be just four wins away.
Andy Pages comes through in the seventh inning to break a tie and four relievers close out a 3-1 victory over the Atlanta Braves to win the NLDS in four games.
Here’s guessing that the NLCS will be the real World Series. And here’s guessing the Dodgers will be ready.
Pages, who won the hearts of Dodger fans last October when he made a leaping game-saving catch over the back of Kiké Hernández, was granted his first big October swing thanks to the Braves largess.
In the seventh inning of a 1-all tie, Teoscar Hernández redeemed himself for another fielding blunder with a single that finally drove dizzying Tyler Mahle from the game.
In came Game 2 rookie sensation Didier Fuentes, only this time, he was all rookie and zero sensation, walking Josue De Paula and Kyle Tucker to load the bases. Considering De Paula is just a kid and Tucker has been struggling, the fact that both showed such patience in such a pressure situation was pretty cool. And moments later, it got even cooler.
In came veteran reliever Robert Suarez, and Pages was ready for him, working the count full before lining the two-run single up the middle.
The Dodgers added a run two innings later on a Max Muncy home run — has there ever been a playoff game when he hasn’t homered? — to finalize the score.
When the game ended on an Austin Riley fly out to right field, Pages celebrated in center field by taking off his cap, turning his face to the sky and pounding the cap three times into his glove.
It was a series that was worth the emotion, the Dodgers famous starting rotation giving up just four runs in 21 ⅓ innings, the bullpen solid behind a revived Edwin Díaz, and the offense doing just enough to beat Braves aces Chris Sale and Mahle.
In the fifth inning of a tie game, starter Tyler Glasnow issued walks to Riley and Michael Harris II. With two out, in came Alex Vesia. Up stepped slugger Matt Olson. The fans climbed to their feet. This was the Braves’ big chance.
But Olson swung at the first pitch and lined it directly to second baseman Kiké Hernández to end the threat and quiet the joint. Díaz threw a hitless ninth for his second save of the series and…who’s going to beat them?
Afterward, Roberts referenced nearly half of his team when talking about his pride. He talked about Pages’ hit, about De Paula’s walk, about reliever Edgardo Henriquez’s 1 ⅔ shutout innings, about Muncy’s bat and Freddie Freeman’s glove
“I guess, amazement,” he said. “Our guys just continue to fight, persevere. You never know who the guy’s going to be.”
The only glaring weakness was, once again, the superstar who used to be their strength. Ohtani scored the Dodgers’ first run after drawing a walk but went hitless in three ensuing at-bats. He only got two hits in the four-game series and you have to wonder if his injury-wracked body would be better out of the lineup.
How well are they playing without the full services of their most historic player? On the verge of making history, the Dodgers don’t even miss him.

item.content:encoded:
8 de octubre de 2026 - 9:55 PM
Atlanta - Andy Pages impulsó dos carreras con un sencillo con las bases llenas en la séptima entrada para darle la ventaja definitiva a Los Ángeles, y los reinante bicampeones Dodgers vencieron el miércoles 4-1 a los Braves de Atlanta para sentenciar su serie divisional de la Liga Nacional.
Los Dodgers ganaron juegos consecutivos en Atlanta para llevarse 3-1 la serie al mejor de cinco y avanzar a la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional dentro de empeño por convertirse en el primer equipo de la Liga Nacional que conquista tres Series Mundiales seguidas.
El cubano Pages conectó una línea por el centro a un lanzamiento en cuenta de 3-2 del venezolano Robert Suárez para remolcar al dominicano Teoscar Hernández, quien había empalmado un sencillo ante el abridor Tyler Mahle, y al corredor emergente Tommy Edman, para poner el 3-1 en el marcador 3-1.
Acto seguido, el colombiano Didier Fuentes concedió base por bolas al bateador emergente dominicano Josue De Paula y a Kyle Tucker para congestionar las bases. Edman corrió por De Paula.
El jonrón solitario de Max Muncy ante el cubano Raisel Iglesias en la novena aumentó la ventaja y dejó al toletero con un gran total de 19 cuadrangulares de postemporada con los Dodgers, ampliando su récord de la franquicia.
El derecho de los Dodgers Tyler Glasnow, en su primera apertura desde el 24 de septiembre, permitió apenas un hit, pero otorgó cinco bases por bolas en cuatro innings y dos tercios.
Después de conceder dos boletos en la quinta, el zurdo Alex Vesia terminó la entrada con un rodado de Matt Olson a la segunda base.
La oportunidad desperdiciada dejó a los Braves con 18 pasaporte en la serie, pero ninguno se concretó en carrera.
Glasnow y cuatro relevistas se combinaron para permitir apenas tres hits. Tanner Scott lanzó una octava entrada perfecta antes de que el puertorriqueño Edwin “Sugar” Díaz sacara tres outs rápidos para apuntarse el salvamento.
Fue el segundo salvamento en noches consecutivas para Díaz, de vuelta en el puesto de cerrador de los Dodgers.
Mahle, originario de Newport Beach, California, y que creció como aficionado de los Dodgers, permitió dos carreras —una limpia— en seis innings y un tercio.
Michael Harris II conectó el primer lanzamiento de Glasnow para un sencillo antes de robarse la segunda y, finalmente, anotar desde tercera con un lanzamiento descontrolado que rebotó en el protector de pecho del receptor Will Smith.
Los Dodgers empataron en la segunda con ayuda de dos errores de Atlanta. Shohei Ohtani recibió base por bolas, se robó la segunda y avanzó a tercera por un tiro desviado del receptor Sean Murphy hacia el jardín central. El elevado de Muncy a la zona corta del jardín izquierdo fue dejado caer por el campocorto hondureño Mauricio Dubón para otro error, lo que permitió que Ohtani anotara.
Hernández se estrelló contra la pared al intentar atrapar el doble de Ozzie Albies ante Vesia para abrir la sexta. Hernández se señaló la cabeza y el cuello al hablar con un preparador físico, pero se mantuvo en el juego.
El venezolano Edgardo Henríquez dejó varado a Albies en segunda. Henríquez permitió un hit al cubrir una entrada y dos tercios sin carrera para llevarse la victoria.
Las noticias explicadas de forma sencilla y directa para entender lo más importante del día.

item.title: [Heavy.com] Dodgers Keep Pushing Off Shohei Ohtani Problem
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers won the NLDS on Wednesday night, needing four games to defeat the Atlanta Braves in the best-of-five series. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers won the NLDS on Wednesday night, needing four games to defeat the Atlanta Braves in the best-of-five series.
That series victory, which the Dodgers hope is the start of their three-peat World Series journey in this postseason, masked something, though. Shohei Ohtani still isn’t right.
The Dodgers have more or less acknowledged this already. After years of not moving him around the batting lineup, they’re moving him around the batting lineup.
And sure, the Dodgers might be so super-powered that it doesn’t even matter if they get Ohtani’s best. In some ways, it feels like they’re unbeatable.
But Ohtani is one of one for a reason. There’s no baseball player on the planet. Even when he’s not able to pitch, at least in the past, his contributions at the plate and on the bases have been otherworldly.
At the moment, though, Ohtani is very human.
What’s Wrong With Shohei Ohtani?
In an injury-plagued season, Ohtani simply appears to still be injured.
The Dodgers aren’t going to go too in-depth on any such speculation, but that doesn’t stop onlookers from feeling like that has to be the case.
The Ringer’s Anthony Dabbundo wrote on X: “It probably won’t matter because dodgers run prevention machine goes brrrr, but Shohei Ohtani hasn’t had a good at bat in any of the first four NLDS games and doesn’t seem healthy.”
That about sums it up. Something just doesn’t seem right with Ohtani.
Ohtani is 2-for-13 so far in the postseason, and that extends to a cold finish to the regular season for him.
For what it’s worth, Ohtani doesn’t yet have an extra-base hit in the small sample of the NLDS.
He went 0-for-3 with a walk and a run in the clinching Game 4.
Even dating back to the regular season, Ohtani is 10 for his last 60 (.167 average) with no home runs in that span.
Dodgers Dilemma
With almost any other hitter on the planet, you’d take an honest look at how he was feeling and consider a change.
It almost feels like Ohtani is above that. Sure, the Dodgers don’t want to hurt him worse, but if he believes he can be in the lineup, L.A. doesn’t want to tell him no.
It puts the Dodgers in tough spots, though. They have to make judgments on how his health might impact his play, except they aren’t inside his body to really know how he’s doing.
And truly, the Dodgers could win it all without Ohtani. So if he’s going to play, he needs to be more helpful than hurtful, because they have other options.
Los Angeles might not be able to solve this. There isn’t a ton of time.
But one way or the other, Ohtani is going to impact what happens in these playoffs. He always does. This year, it just might look a little different.

item.title: [New York Post] Doctober classic propels Dodgers to NLCS in quest for World Series three-peat
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez

item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA — Dave Roberts didn’t hesitate.
So what if Tyler Glasnow had thrown only 78 pitches?
So what if he was still in the fifth inning?
Glasnow had walked his second batter of the inning, and Roberts wasn’t about to take any chances.
Calling on Alex Vesia to record the final out of the inning, Roberts initiated a chaotic sequence of events that resulted in the Dodgers claiming a 4-1 victory over the Braves in Game 4 of their National League Division Series.
The Dodgers advanced to the NL Championship Series.
Because of Tarik Skubal.
Because of Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
Because of Freddie Freeman.
And because of David Ray Roberts, the manager affectionately known as Doc who has a game or two like this every October.
The victory over the Braves on Wednesday was a Doctober classic.
On a day in which one of his four aces lasted only 4 ⅔ innings, Roberts figured out how to cover 13 outs of the game with a notoriously unpredictable bullpen.
Roberts’ fingerprints were also all over Andy Pages’ two-run single in the seventh inning that broke open the game.
When Teoscar Hernandez singled that inning with one out, Braves manager Walt Weiss replaced starting pitcher Tyler Mahle with right-hander Didier Fuentes.
Fuentes forced Max Muncy to ground out, but Hernandez advanced to second base on the play.
Due up was Game 3 hero Kike Hernandez.
Rather than have the right-handed utilityman face Fuentes, Roberts deployed rookie Josue De Paula as a pinch hitter. The left-handed-hitting De Paula drew a walk, at which point he was replaced on the basepaths by Tommy Edman.
Kyle Tucker followed up with another walk to load the bases, at which point Weiss turned to fireballer Robert Suarez to pitch to Pages.
Pages batted .078 in the postseason last year, which resulted in his benching in the World Series. He was 0-for-7 in the first two games of this series, but Roberts stuck with him.
Roberts’ faith was rewarded by the most important hit of Pages’ three-year career, a single to right field that drove in two runs to push the Dodgers in front, 3-1. The runs were the Dodgers’ first of the series that weren’t scored via a home run.
The manager demonstrated an equal level of creativity in directing his bullpen.
Vesia returned for the sixth inning, only to give up a leadoff double to Ozzie Albies. Roberts kept the left-hander in for another batter, the left-handed-hitting Drake Baldwin, who lined out.
Roberts’ next call to the bullpen was for Edgardo Henriquez, who spent the last two weeks of the regular season on the injured list. Henriquez gave up a run in the Dodgers’ Game 2 loss, but not only did Roberts trust him to prevent Albies from scoring, he also had him pitch the seventh inning.
From there, it was simple.
Tanner Scott pitched the eighth inning. With Muncy homering in the ninth inning to increase the lead to 4-1, Edwin Diaz came in to record the last three outs.
The Dodgers moved to within four wins of playing in their third consecutive World Series, and they did it with Shohei Ohtani still missing in action.
Ohtani was 2-for-13 in this series.
“It’s good to know that we can still win games without him doing a whole bunch,” Roberts said. “But he’s going to come to life. It will happen.”
Roberts has squinted extra hard in recent days to find evidence of that.
Here’s the reality: In his last 22 combined games between the regular season and playoffs, Ohtani has no home runs and only one RBI.
That isn’t a slump.
The No. 1 player in the game doesn’t go this long without hitting in the prime of his career without something being seriously wrong with him.
Ohtani spent 15 days last month on the injured list because of a discomfort in his right arm. A couple of days before he was placed on the IL, he said his left knee was also bothering him.
The uncertainty over Ohtani’s capabilities forced Roberts to move him around the lineup.
With Mookie Betts grinding out quality at-bats as the leadoff hitter and Freeman producing enough to solidify his place as the team’s No. 2 hitter, Ohtani was removed from the top of the order.
Against the left-handed Chris Sale in Game 3, Ohtani batted fifth. Against the right-handed Mahle on Wednesday, he batted cleanup.
Ohtani managed to create something out of nothing in the second inning. He drew a walk, then stole second base, prompting Braves catcher Sean Murphy to airmail a throw into center field. Ohtani scampered to third base. When Braves shortstop Mauricio Dubón dropped a popup by Muncy in shallow left field, Ohtani scored to tie the game at 1.
Ohtani didn’t collect any hits Wednesday, but he didn’t have to.
Roberts had the game under control.

item.title: [Field Level Media] Andy Pages' clutch hit sends Dodgers past Braves, into NLCS
item.description: ATLANTA — Andy Pages’ two-run single in the seventh inning broke open a pitchers’ duel and helped the Los Angeles Dodgers close out their National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves with a 4-1 win in Game 4 on Wednesday. The Dodgers, who won the series 3-1 and are looking to be the first National League team to win three straight World Series, await the winner of the other NLDS between the Brewers and Padres. Milwaukee leads that best-of-five set 2-1 entering a Wednesday matchup i
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA — Andy Pages’ two-run single in the seventh inning broke open a pitchers’ duel and helped the Los Angeles Dodgers close out their National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves with a 4-1 win in Game 4 on Wednesday.
The Dodgers, who won the series 3-1 and are looking to be the first National League team to win three straight World Series, await the winner of the other NLDS between the Brewers and Padres. Milwaukee leads that best-of-five set 2-1 entering a Wednesday matchup in San Diego.
Pages’ hit was Los Angeles’ first with runners in scoring position in the series after the team started 0-for-14. It came off of Robert Suarez after Teoscar Hernandez hit a one-out single against Braves starter Tyler Mahle and then reliever Didier Fuentes issued back-to-back two-out walks.
Pages had two of the Dodgers’ five hits and two of their three RBIs in the win.
His clutch hit came the inning after Atlanta got nothing out of Ozzie Albies’ leadoff double, with Edgardo Henriquez (1-0) escaping the jam to earn his first career postseason victory.
Los Angeles’ Max Muncy tacked on an insurance run with a solo homer in the ninth, his third long ball of the postseason.
Mahle (0-1) was a tough-luck loser, charged with two runs (one earned) on three hits over 6 1/3 innings. He struck out four and walked one.
Michael Harris II had two of Atlanta’s three hits, including a double. However, the Braves’ situational hitting issues continued as they finished the series 1-for-23 with runners in scoring position.
Dodgers right-hander Tyler Glasnow battled through 4 1/3 innings, allowing just one run on one hit, walking five and striking out five. Alex Vesia, Henriquez, Tanner Scott and Edwin Diaz followed and combined to allow no runs on two hits over the final 4 1/3 innings, setting down the final seven Atlanta batters in a row.
Diaz earned his second save of the series.
Los Angeles’ pitching staff gave up eight runs on 18 hits over the four-game series.
The Braves opened the scoring in the bottom of the first on a wild pitch that scored Harris. He led off with a single, stole second and moved to third on a fielder’s choice.
The Dodgers equalized in the second behind a pair of Braves errors. Shohei Ohtani drew a leadoff walk, stole second and moved to third on an errant throw from catcher Sean Murphy. Muncy then hit a sky-high popup to shallow left that shortstop Mauricio Dubon dropped, allowing Ohtani to score.
–Curt Weiler, Field Level Media

item.title: [Orange County Register] Andy Pages comes through in the clutch to send Dodgers to NLCS
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett

item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA — Overmatched last postseason and benched during the World Series, Andy Pages used the embarrassment to fuel an All-Star season in 2026.
But he was hit by a pitch on Aug. 21 that broke a bone in his hand, didn’t return until the final six games of the regular season and started the postseason, trying to do too much (by his manager’s estimation) to make up for last fall’s lack of contributions.
The accounts have been reconciled. It was Pages’ clutch two-out, two-run single in the seventh inning that broke a tie and lifted the Dodgers to a 4-1 victory on Wednesday night in Game 4 of their National League Division Series with the Atlanta Braves.
The victory sends the Dodgers to the National League Championship Series against either the Milwaukee Brewers or San Diego Padres. The Dodgers have reached baseball’s Final Four for the fifth time in the past seven years, the eighth time in the past 11. Their quest for a ‘three-peat’ will continue Sunday either in Milwaukee or at home against the Padres.
This series was decided in the seventh inning.
With the score tied 1-1, Teoscar Hernandez – fresh off a collision with the left field wall that left him on the warning track dirt, rubbing the left side of his head – singled with one out off Braves starter Tyler Mahle. It was just the third hit off Mahle and it came on just his 85th pitch. But Braves manager Walt Weiss went to his bullpen, bringing in Game 2 hero Didier Fuentes to face Max Muncy.
Fuentes got Muncy to ground out, Hernandez moving to second, but he walked pinch-hitter Josue De Paula and Kyle Tucker to load the bases with two outs.
Weiss had a quick hook, pulling Fuentes and handing the ball to veteran Robert Suarez to face Pages. Pages got ahead in the count, 3-and-1, then swung and missed at a 99.1 mph fastball from Suarez. He got another fastball on the full count and didn’t miss, stroking it through the middle for the Dodgers’ first – and only hit – with a runner in scoring position in their 16 at-bats in those situations during the four games of this series.
Runs had been hard to come by in Atlanta. After Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Chris Sale squared off in Game 3, Mahle and Tyler Glasnow allowed just a dirty run each through the first six innings.
In the bottom of the first, Michael Harris II led off with a single off of Glasnow. He stole second, went to third on a ground out and score when Glasnow spiked a knuckle curve in the dirt well in front of home plate. It bounced off Will Smith’s chest protector back towards the mound and Glasnow couldn’t retrieve it in time to get Harris.
In the top of the second, Shohei Ohtani took a five-pitch walk, stole second and went to third when Braves catcher Sean Murphy threw the ball into center field. Ohtani scored when Braves shortstop Mauricio Dubon dropped Max Muncy’s pop-up in shallow left field.
Mahle struck out only four in his 6⅓ innings (three of them consecutively in the fourth inning) and got just seven swings-and-misses on 95 pitches. But he got a lot of soft contact – and when he didn’t, it usually found a Braves fielder’s glove. The Dodgers hit seven balls in the first six innings with exit velocities of 95 mph or higher (the StatCast standard for “hard-hit”). Only one of them was a base hit – Pages’ third-inning single (106.7 mph).
Against Glasnow, the Braves just didn’t make much contact at all.
He gave up that leadoff single to Harris in the first inning but no other hits. He did walk five, though, including two in the fifth inning that prompted Manager Dave Roberts to pull him from the game after 78 pitches.
Dodgers pitchers somehow walked 18 batters in the series but let none of them score. Alex Vesia retired Matt Olson to end that fifth inning. Edgardo Henriquez held the Braves scoreless over the next two. Tanner Scott retired the slumping heart of the Braves’ order and Muncy gave Edwin Diaz cushion in the ninth inning with a solo home run (his 19th career postseason homer, a franchise record).
More to come on this story.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Andy Pages single beats Braves, Dodgers win NLDS in 4 games
item.dc:creator: Eric Stephen
item.description: It took until the seventh inning of the fourth game of the National League Division Series for the Dodgers to get their first hit with a runner in scoring position. But Andy Pages made it count, with a two-run single to break a tie in a 4-1 win over the Atlanta Braves on Wednesday night at Truist Park, clinching the NLCS to send the Dodgers to their third National League Championship Series in a row. The winning rally started with a single by Teoscar Hernández, just minutes after crashing into t
item.content:encoded:
It took until the seventh inning of the fourth game of the National League Division Series for the Dodgers to get their first hit with a runner in scoring position. But Andy Pages made it count, with a two-run single to break a tie in a 4-1 win over the Atlanta Braves on Wednesday night at Truist Park, clinching the NLCS to send the Dodgers to their third National League Championship Series in a row.
The winning rally started with a single by Teoscar Hernández, just minutes after crashing into the left field wall on a Braves double in the previous half-inning. That ended the night for Tyler Mahle, who continued to have the Dodgers number, once again pitching into the seventh.
In came Game 2 Braves hero Didier Fuentes, whose second batter faced was fellow 21-year-old pinch-hitter Josue De Paula, only 24 days his senior. De Paula, in just his second postseason plate appearance, walked, then was removed for pinch-runner Tommy Edman. Kyle Tucker also walked to load the bases, setting up Pages — the Dodgers RBI leader this season — to single home a pair.
After going hitless in his first two games this series, Pages had two hits in Game 3 and two more in Game 4, equaling his total for the entire postseason in 2025. The hit also snapped an 0-for-14 skid by the Dodgers with runners in scoring position to start this series.
The first of those runs snapped a string of 22 straight innings by Mahle against the Dodgers without allowing an earned run, dating all the way back to 2022.
Edgardo Henriquez, who entered with one out in the sixth inning and stranded a runner on second, followed with a scoreless seventh inning to bookend the Dodgers rally, and earned the win.
Just like in Game 3, Tanner Scott pitched a scoreless eighth and Edwin Díaz closed out the win in the ninth, giving the Dodgers the planned back end of their bullpen that hadn't really been fully intact since early April.
Dodgers pitchers allowed eight total runs in the four-game series.
Max power
Max Muncy added some insurance with a solo home run in the ninth inning, extending his Dodgers career postseason record with now 19 home runs. Muncy also homered in Games 1 and 2 of this series, matching his most prolific postseason series with the long ball. He also hit three home runs in the 2019 NLDS against the Washington Nationals.
Sloppy start
Both teams exchanged mistakes for each other's first run, including an errant throw into center field on a stolen base attempt from each side. Michael Harris II got a great jump from third base on a wild pitch by Tyler Glasnow that didn't get too far from home plate in the first inning, catching the Dodgers flat-footed. In the top of the second, Shohei Ohtani walked, stole second and went to third on the bad throw, then scored when a Max Muncy popup into short left field was biffed by shortstop Mauricio Dubón.
Glasnow improved a bit as the game progressed, and didn't allow another hit after Harris led off the game with a single. But, like Blake Snell in Game 2, Glasnow on Wednesday walked five batters, including two in the fifth inning — a leadoff free pass to Austin Riley after getting ahead 0-2, and a two-out, four-pitch walk to Ronald Acuña Jr. to end Glasnow's night early.
The Dodgers right-hander struck out five with those five walks in his 4 2/3 innings, and like Snell limited the damage to only one run. Alex Vesia helped, inducing a groundout to second base to end the fifth inning with those two Glasnow walks left stranded on base, and the game still tied.
Glasnow threw 78 pitches, 44 for strikes.
Not so free passes
None of Glasnow's five walks in Game 4 scored, and none of the 18 Braves who walked in the NLDS have touched home plate. But there have still been costs to that Dodgers wildness. For one, the Dodgers had to turn to its bullpen much earlier than hoped in two of the four games.
Also, two of Snell's walks in the first inning of Game 2, pushing Acuña to third base, which allowed him to score on an infield single. In Game 3, the pinch-hit walk by Rowdy Tellez pushed Dubón to third base, which allowed him to score on a groundout. So the walks have been costly, even if not as much as perhaps they should have been.
NLDS Game 4 particulars
Home run: Max Muncy (3)
WP — Edgardo Henriquez (1-0): 1 2/3 IP, 1 hit
LP — Tyler Mahle (0-1): 6 1/3 IP, 3 hits, 2 runs (1 earned), 1 walk, 4 strikeouts
Sv — Edwin Díaz (2): 1 IP, 1 strikeout
Up next
The Dodgers move on to a third consecutive National League Championship Series, and eighth in the last 11 years, beginning Sunday night (time TBD, Fox Sports) either in Milwaukee against the Brewers or at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles against the Padres.

item.title: [The Atlanta Journal-Constitution] The Win Column: Is Freddie Freeman now an Atlanta villain?
item.dc:creator: Ken Sugiura
item.description: Greetings, Tyler Estep enthusiasts! You’ll be pleased to know that the admired and capable Tyler will be back next week. This will be my second and final missive in his estimable place. But enough blathering. On with the newsletter. I apologize in advance that I’m not as concise as Tyler, but I make up for it in by being less funny. HOW ARE WE FEELING ABOUT FREDDIE FREEMAN? If you watched Tuesday’s broadcast of Game 3 of the NLDS between the Braves and the Dodgers or were at Truist Park, surely
item.content:encoded:
Greetings, Tyler Estep enthusiasts!
You’ll be pleased to know that the admired and capable Tyler will be back next week. This will be my second and final missive in his estimable place.
But enough blathering. On with the newsletter. I apologize in advance that I’m not as concise as Tyler, but I make up for it in by being less funny.
HOW ARE WE FEELING ABOUT FREDDIE FREEMAN?
If you watched Tuesday’s broadcast of Game 3 of the NLDS between the Braves and the Dodgers or were at Truist Park, surely you heard the boos raining down on the longtime Brave when he came to the plate.
I was fascinated by this. On social media — granted, not the best barometer for anything except for measuring people’s capacity for surliness to complete strangers — there was a lot of chatter from fans about how Freeman cannot be welcomed back like the prodigal son, as has been the case since he signed with the Dodgers before the 2022 season.
At least not in the playoffs, his first at Truist in Dodgers colors.
It was a reasonable (and evidently popular) position to take, although I don’t know why there has to be a group think about this.
But the interesting thing to me was that the response went all the other way, to where he was getting booed with more intensity than anyone except maybe Shohei Ohtani.
I had thought the switch would just be from applause to indifference.
But it was like he went from “guy we still love” to “guy we now despise.”
It was almost like a scene out of a movie, where the boy has a dog he can no longer keep as a pet but the dog still follows him around so the boy tearfully has to turn on the dog (“Now, git! You hear me!”) to make it clear that he is no longer wanted. (That was weirdly specific, I realize.)
Was it because he left the Braves or because he’s one of the Dodgers’ best players (he did homer) or my own movie/dog/boy interpretation?
This was Freeman’s explanation, as reported in a story worth reading by colleague and longtime Freeman chronicler Gabe Burns:
“I’ve got a gray uniform on, I expect boos.”
Eager to hear your thoughts.
A DREAM SCENARIO
You may have missed this, but the Dream made a rather newsy announcement Tuesday. They will play all of their home games at State Farm Arena next season (and at least the one following) after playing for the past six seasons at Gateway Center Arena (capacity: 3,575, smallest in the WNBA).
The Dream liked the College Park arena but it was too small to be sustainable. But another aspect of it was, as much as they liked bragging about selling out Gateway Center, it was difficult to ascertain what the demand would be in a larger arena.
Ever since the team’s inception in 2008, they’ve had trouble drawing, even when they’ve had competitive teams, starting at State Farm (then Philips Arena).
But a telling moment came when the Dream played at State Farm in June against a non-marquee opponent (the Toronto Tempo) on a Monday night. In recent seasons, they’ve moved games to State Farm for surefire draws like Caitlyn Clark’s Indiana Fever and the Las Vegas Aces.
Team president and chief operating officer Morgan Shaw Parker told me then that “this is a way for us to really test that out and understand the market a little better. Because you can’t just understand if you’re only bringing in one (visiting) team to play (in State Farm).”
The Dream-Tempo game drew nearly 10,000.
That and other indicators evidently informed the ownership group that it was time to take the next step. It’s great for fans of the team and women’s basketball in general.
A team spokesperson told me Tuesday that it’s not yet decided if they’ll use a smaller configuration as they did for Game 1 of the WNBA semifinals on Sunday or use the full configuration.
It wouldn’t surprise me if it was a mixture. And the team’s ownership continues to explore having its own arena. (Georgia State Convocation Center makes a lot of sense to me.)
The Dream and New York Liberty play Game 2 of their WNBA semifinal series Wednesday night at State Farm. They are using the smaller configuration (closing off most of the upper deck) because of, I was told, the quick turnaround for playoff ticket sales.
Game 1 drew 9,745 and the get-in price for Game 2 on Seatgeek on Wednesday morning was $98.
A new chapter is beginning.
KIRBY SMART ASKED, WE ANSWERED
This is something of an homage to the very capable Tyler, whose work I really appreciate for the way he approaches sports. Saturday, after Georgia whipped up on Vanderbilt, Bulldogs coach Kirby Smart was asked about a particular officiating call on quarterback Gunner Stockton.
Smart declined to offer his evaluation of the call, saying “the last thing I do is judge officials,” which, if you’ve ever seen a Georgia game or are an SEC official, you may quibble with.
But he went on to explain his non-judging stance by saying he doesn’t even know — for instance, when a punt is shanked out of bounds — how officials determine where to spot the ball.
I saw that and thought: A) I am always intrigued by how Smart’s mind works, and B) This is prime Win Column material.
And so I sought out an answer.
Big thanks to former longtime SEC official Gus Morris, who delivered perfectly.
Per Morris (whose “Saturdays in the South” book about his life as an SEC official is great): “The referee is positioned near the punter and then, after the ball is punted away, goes to the punter’s spot. If the ball is punted out of bounds, he notes where it landed to establish the flight path of the ball.”
An official lined up deep downfield on the sideline (there’s one on each) starts to move up toward the line of scrimmage with an eye on the referee. (Not that important, but this “Where’s he going to stop?” march has always made me think of the mountain-climber game on “The Price is Right.” If you know, you know.)
“When he intersects with the line that the referee establishes, then you’ll see the referee (drop his raised arm) and then the deep-wing official will stop there and establish the spot there,” Morris told me. “It’s not just arbitrarily determined. There’s actually a mechanic that handles that situation.”
I thought that was pretty interesting. Hope you did, too.
At the Win Column, we are all Kirby Smart.
A SHOUTOUT TO MY DAD
To my chagrin, I will miss the remainder of the Braves NLDS and the Georgia-Alabama game because I will be off from this afternoon through Sunday for a great reason. My father, Go Sugiura, is turning 90 on Sunday and my family will be flying to San Francisco to help celebrate.
Among many other things, my dad fostered my love for sports and helped me on my path to this job. He gave me countless weekend afternoons in our backyard in Northfield, Illinois, playing catch and throwing batting practice in the spring and summer and tossing the football in the fall. I didn’t realize it then, but those were truly some of the best days of my life.
Serendipitously, he was able to get two Bears season tickets for the 1984 and 1985 seasons, the latter proving to be only arguably the greatest in NFL history, and we went to nearly all of them together. (Amusingly, my dad’s friend who gave up the tickets for those two years because the Bears had forever been mediocre wanted them back after that and then they didn’t go to another Super Bowl for almost 20 years.)
And while my dad knew little about the newspaper business and had no connections to leverage, he did what he could.
When I was in college, rather randomly, he ended up sharing an office floor with Walter Payton and, surely knowing he couldn’t ask for too many favors, spent one of them asking him if he could talk with me and share advice about journalism from his perspective as a former professional athlete. (Which Payton graciously did, and I still think back to.)
I went to Japan (my parents’ country of origin) after I graduated to study and travel (a trip my parents funded) and, as I began to look for a job upon my return, heard from The Philadelphia Inquirer.
I went to Philadelphia for an interview and when I met with an editor, she mentioned talking to my dad (because I’d left our home phone as my contact information) and smilingly referred to him as “your agent,” which I’m sure meant that he, as is his way, had been responsive, thorough and eager in his communication.
I didn’t get a job there immediately, and as I looked for a job after returning home, I remember he bought a CD-ROM (this was 1995) with the address of, literally, every publication in the United States.
Even, like, Cat Fancy magazine.
And his plan was that I was going to write to all of them to find a job. He set up a mail merge and the address labels and everything.
Thankfully, we didn’t follow through completely on this strategy, as it may have resulted in me becoming the unwitting cub reporter of Crocheting Monthly or some such.
Regardless, it was an expression of love that I cherish still.
Happy birthday, Dad. And thank you.
PHOTO OF THE DAY
Thanks for reading to the very bottom of the Win Column. Questions, comments, ideas? Contact me at tyler.estep@ajc.com (or me, Ken, at ken.sugiura@ajc.com)
Until next time.
Ken Sugiura is a sports columnist at the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. Formerly the Georgia Tech beat reporter, Sugiura started at the AJC in 1998 and has covered a variety of beats, mostly within sports.

item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers are back in Atlanta for Game 4 of the NLDS on Wednesday, needing just one more win to clinch the series. After getting to Chris Sale in Game 3, the Dodgers will face right-hander Tyler Mahle, who has turned heads since being acquired at the trade deadline from the San Francisco Giants.
After batting fifth in the starting lineup for the first time as a Dodger, Shohei Ohtani will once again be hitting in the middle third of the order, this time moving up to the cleanup spot with Teoscar Hernández sliding down to the fifth spot in the order.
Max Muncy makes his first start this series since batting 8th in Game 1 against left-hander Dylan Dodd, this time batting sixth in the lineup with Miguel Rojas getting the day off after dealing with back tightness. The hero of Game 3 on offense, Kiké Hernández, makes his second straight start, this time batting seventh while getting the start at second base. Kyle Tucker once again hits in the 8 spot while Andy Pages rounds things out after a multi-hit performance.
Runs have been hard to come by so far this series, as the Dodgers have plated just 10 combined runs over their first three postseason games, all of which have come via home runs. The main Achilles heel for the Dodgers has been their consistent inability to produce with runners in scoring position, as the team is 0-13 in those situations. The Braves, to their credit, have managed to get one hit with runners in scoring position, albeit across 14 at-bats, and have combined to score just eight runs over the first three games.
The Dodgers have fared well in previous matchups against Mahle, as the right-hander has a combined 3-3 record with a 3.15 ERA. Most of the damage came when Mahle was still with the Cincinnati Reds, and in his most recent start against the Dodgers back when he was with San Francisco, he shut them down over seven shutout innings in a 3-0 Giants win on April 22. Since joining Atlanta, Mahle finished the regular season with a 1.99 ERA and limited the Philadelphia Phillies to just one run in his most recent Wild Card start.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are coming off a massive Game 3 victory over the Atlanta Braves on the road at Truist Park on Tuesday night.
They’ll now take a 2-1 series lead into Wednesday’s matchup and sit just one win away from advancing to the NLCS as they continue to chase a third consecutive World Series title.
Ahead of the matchup. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts elected to make some changes to his starting lineup for the second straight day.
Dodgers Announce Teoscar Hernandez Change
Among those moving in the order is slugger Teoscar Hernandez, who hit third in the lineup Tuesday and will now drop to sixth for Game 4.
Hernandez is coming off back-to-back 0-for-4 performances. And Roberts will move catcher Will Smith into the No. 3 spot, while Shohei Ohtani moves from fifth to fourth and will bat cleanup.
Max Muncy will bat fifth in the lineup after starting Tuesday’s game on the bench.
Here’s the Dodgers starting lineup:
Via Underdog MLB: “Dodgers 10/7 M. Betts SS F. Freeman 1B W. Smith C S. Ohtani DH T. Hernández LF M. Muncy 3B E. Hernández 2B K. Tucker RF A. Pages CF T. Glasnow SP.”

W. Smith C

T. Hernández LF
M. Muncy 3B
E. Hernández 2B
K. Tucker RF

— Underdog MLB (@UnderdogMLB) October 7, 2026
Looking at the Dodgers
L.A. has relied heavily on the long ball for its offense so far in this series against Atlanta.
After winning 5-3 in Game 1, losing 3-2 in Game 2 on Sunday and then winning 3-1 on Tuesday, all 10 of their combined runs in the series have come via home runs.
And they’ve seemingly done it with Shohei Ohtani being pretty much a non-factor at the plate.

item.title: [Dodger Blue] Dave Roberts shares Shohei Ohtani's reaction to being dropped in Dodgers lineup

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts decided to drop Shohei Ohtani to fifth in the lineup for Game 3 of the National League Division Series amid the designated hitter’s ongoing struggles.
Ohtani was 2-for-8 in the series entering play Tuesday against the Atlanta Braves. Having a tough left-handed assignment on the mound in Chris Sale influenced Roberts’ decision, and Ohtani completely bought in.
“Runs are going to be hard to come by. We all understand that,” Roberts began. “Sale’s going to be tough. But the guys I feel at the top have a good chance to get on base, and I do think that there’s going to be opportunities where the game, the situation, bleeds into Shohei’s at-bat.
“So I had a good conversation with him last night, told him my thoughts. And he completely understood and in all honesty, he said, ‘I was going to come to you in September and say, why don’t you hit me seventh?’ My point being, he wants to do whatever will help the team.
“So I feel good about this today. And it’s nothing as a sign of what’s more to come. It’s just for today specifically.”
The flow of the game played perfectly into the Dodgers’ strategy, as Ohtani was given prime RBI opportunities twice within the first three innings. But the results were not what Roberts had hoped for.
The Dodgers’ star struck out in the first inning to strand a runner in scoring position, but he did reach on catcher’s interference later in the third.
Because of the relationships Roberts has built with his players, he was not surprised Ohtani took the news well. While it was a difficult decision, Roberts felt it gave his team the best chance to counter Sale and the pitchers coming in after him.
“Not surprised at all. And I think that from day one, I’ve always said that my job is to do whatever is best for the team. And so I know I’ve built the equity and the trust in the players,” he said. “And so today I just feel this gives us the best chance to beat the Braves today and combat Sale, to combat what they’re going to throw after Sale. I feel good about it.”
The Dodgers’ skipper also hoped the change would help Ohtani stay within himself better than he has.
“I use that a lot, where it might give him a different look, let the game come to him a little bit later. I don’t think it’s a pressure thing. I do think it’s something where he wants to do more. But in that same breath, I do think that there’s going to be a couple big spots today where he’s going to be at-bat,” Roberts said.
Although Sale presents a wholly unique challenge for any left-handed hitter, Ohtani chased plenty out of the zone in the first inning. The Braves starter attacked the outside part of the plate and effectively tunneled his fastball and slider to get Ohtani to chase.
Ohtani worked a 3-0 count in his third at-bat against Sale but lost a challenge on what he thought was ball four and proceeded to get beaten by a fastball inside for a flyout.
Rather than signaling a lack of confidence, Roberts believes Ohtani nearly initiating the lineup change himself is an example of self-scouting.
“He’s a very good self-evaluator, a very high competitor and expects a lot from himself. I still think he’s very confident. But Sale’s a different monster. He’s tough, certainly, against lefties. But I still think he’s confident,” Roberts said.
“So now with that, just getting him back in the zone, and that’s easier said than done, I understand that. But there’s going to be high velocity trying to crowd him in to then spin him off. Is Shohei willing to take the knock to left field as he did against Dodd? So those are the things you’re looking for tonight.”
Shohei Ohtani’s lineup spot in Game 4
The Braves have right-hander Tyler Mahle on the mound to start against Tyler Glasnow in Game 4. However, Roberts said that does not necessarily guarantee that Ohtani will be back in the leadoff spot.
“Mahle is certainly a neutral, you could argue a reverse. So I don’t know that answer. Yes, he does throw with his right hand, but I haven’t made that decision quite yet,” he said.
Roberts did not specify if Ohtani’s at-bats on Thursday would tip the scale one way or the other, but the Dodgers’ skipper did confirm that the left-hander would not be batting in the fifth spot again.
If you love our reporting, choose DodgerBlue.com as a preferred source on Google.

item.title: [El Nuevo Día] ¡Boricuas brillan en octubre! Kike Hernández jonronea y Edwin Díaz salva juego en Atlanta
item.dc:creator: Charles Odum
item.description: 7 de octubre de 2026 - 9:45 PM Atlanta - Yoshinobu Yamamoto ponchó a 10 bateadores en siete entradas, Enrique “Kike” Hernández conectó un jonrón de dos carreras y los Dodgers de Los Ángeles vencieron 3-1 a los Braves de Atlanta el martes por la noche, tomando una ventaja de 2-1 en su Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional. item.content:encoded:
7 de octubre de 2026 - 9:45 PM
Atlanta - Yoshinobu Yamamoto ponchó a 10 bateadores en siete entradas, Enrique “Kike” Hernández conectó un jonrón de dos carreras y los Dodgers de Los Ángeles vencieron 3-1 a los Braves de Atlanta el martes por la noche, tomando una ventaja de 2-1 en su Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional.
Hernández, quien suele brillar en octubre, sacudió su decimoséptimo cuadrangular en postemporada, quebrando un empate con el miembro del Salón de la Fama de Béisbol Carlos Beltrán.
El boricua ahora está empate con Jim Thome, Aaron Judge y David Ortiz en la lista de jonrones en la postemporada.
Yamamoto dominó el muy esperado duelo contra el as de Atlanta, Chris Sale, quien permitió tres carreras y siete imparables en cinco entradas. Yamamoto, Jugador Más Valioso (MVP) de la Serie Mundial de 2025, concedió solo cuatro hits y una base por bolas, mejorando su récord de postemporada a 8-1.
Los Dodgers pueden ganar la serie —pactada al mejor de cinco juegos— y dar un paso más en su intento de convertirse en el primer equipo de la Liga Nacional en ganar tres títulos consecutivos de Serie Mundial si vencen nuevamente a los Braves el miércoles por la noche en el cuarto partido.
Los Braves esperaban que dar descanso adicional a Sale fuera una fórmula ganadora para este crucial tercer encuentro. Sin embargo, tras dejar a seis corredores en base en las primeras tres entradas, permitió el jonrón de dos carreras de Hernández y un cuadrangular solitario de Freddie Freeman en el cuarto episodio.
Ozzie Albies abrió la novena entrada de Atlanta con un doblete contra el muro entre el jardín derecho y el central ante los lanzamientos de Edwin Díaz, avanzando a tercera base tras un rodado de out de Michael Harris II. Díaz dejó al corredor varado cuando Mauricio Dubón fue puesto out en un elevado de foul al jardín derecho y Mike Yastrzemski fue retirado con un rodado al campocorto Mookie Betts.
Tras una temporada agobiado por lesiones, Díaz se apuntó su primer salvado desde el pasado 14 de agosto, cuando lanzó la novena entrada en blanco contra Milwaukee.
FUe además su primer rescate de postemporada desde el 14 de octubre de 2024, cuanto se apuntó un salvamento por los Mets de Nueva York contra los propios Dodgers en la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional.
Dubón realizó una atrapada saltando sobre la barda del jardín izquierdo para robarle un jonrón a Freeman en la tercera entrada; sin embargo, Freeman logró conectar su cuadrangular una entrada más tarde. El jonrón de Hernández hacia el jardín izquierdo impulsó a Andy Pages, quien había conectado un sencillo. Un out después, Freeman conectó el jonrón número 18 de su carrera en postemporada hacia el jardín derecho, ampliando la ventaja a 3-0.
El mánager de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts, bajó al bateador designado Shohei Ohtani al quinto puesto del orden al bate, debido a que Ohtani registraba un promedio de 3 de 15 en su carrera contra Sale. Ohtani se había ido de 4-0 con dos ponches ante Sale cuando los Dodgers perdieron 1-0 el 26 de agosto en Atlanta. Roberts predijo acertadamente que Ohtani tendría oportunidades con corredores en base al batear en una posición más baja del orden de bateo.
En la primera entrada, con corredores en primera y segunda, Sale ponchó a Ohtani para cerrar el episodio. En la tercera, con dos corredores en base, Ohtani llegó a primera gracias a una interferencia del receptor Drake Baldwin —lo que llenó las bases—, antes de que Miguel Rojas terminara la entrada con un elevado al jardín derecho. Ohtani recibió una base por bolas al abrir la octava entrada frente a Brent Suter, el cuarto lanzador de Atlanta.
Un rodado de Baldwin a primera base, con las bases llenas, impulsó a Dubón —quien había conectado un sencillo— en la quinta entrada, anotando así la única carrera de Atlanta ante Yamamoto.
Rojas abandonó el partido durante un turno al bate en la octava entrada. El segunda base pareció lastimarse la espalda al realizar un swing y fue sustituido por Tommy Edman. Los Dodgers informaron que la lesión consistía en dolor en la zona lumbar.
Tanner Scott sumó dos ponches en una octava entrada sin anotaciones para Los Ángeles.
Las noticias explicadas de forma sencilla y directa para entender lo más importante del día.

item.title: [WSLS] Yamamoto is dominant again as Dodgers ride homers from Hernández and Freeman to 3-1 win over Braves
item.dc:creator: Charles Odum; Associated Press
item.description: ATLANTA – Yoshinobu Yamamoto felt trust from Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts when he remained in a crucial NL Division Series game after a stressful fifth inning. “I’d like to continue living up to the highest expectation,” Yamamoto said through a translator. Recommended Videos The right-hander from Japan continues to do more than just meet expectations in the postseason. Yamamoto struck out 10 in seven brilliant innings, Kiké Hernández hit a two-run homer and the Dodgers beat the Atlan
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA – Yoshinobu Yamamoto felt trust from Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts when he remained in a crucial NL Division Series game after a stressful fifth inning.
“I’d like to continue living up to the highest expectation,” Yamamoto said through a translator.
Recommended Videos
The right-hander from Japan continues to do more than just meet expectations in the postseason.
Yamamoto struck out 10 in seven brilliant innings, Kiké Hernández hit a two-run homer and the Dodgers beat the Atlanta Braves 3-1 on Tuesday night to take a 2-1 lead in their NL Division Series.
Yamamoto dominated his much-anticipated matchup with Atlanta ace Chris Sale, who allowed three runs and seven hits in five innings. Last year's World Series MVP permitted only four hits and one walk while improving to 8-1 with a 2.14 ERA in 11 career postseason outings, including 10 starts.
His 10 strikeouts were a postseason high for him.
“I was confident and able to control all my pitches today,” Yamamoto said.
The Dodgers can clinch the best-of-five series and take another step toward becoming the first National League team to win three consecutive World Series by beating the Braves again Wednesday night in Game 4.
Atlanta hoped giving Sale extra rest would be a winning formula in the pivotal third game. Instead, after stranding six runners in the first three innings, he gave up the two-run homer to Hernández and a solo shot to former Braves star Freddie Freeman in the fourth.
“He was still touching 100 (mph),” manager Walt Weiss said of Sale. “The stuff was fine. Like I said, maybe the command not perfect. It wasn’t bad. But they did a nice job against him.”
That was all the offensive support Yamamoto and relievers Tanner Scott and Edwin Díaz would need.
Ozzie Albies opened the Atlanta ninth with a double off the right-center wall against Díaz and moved to third on Michael Harris II's groundout. Díaz stranded the runner and earned a save when Mauricio Dubón fouled out to right field and Mike Yastrzemski grounded out to shortstop Mookie Betts.
A homer for the boo birds
Freeman said he didn't mind being booed by Atlanta fans in the sellout crowd of 42,420.
“I’ve got a gray uniform on,” Freeman said. “I expect boos. It’s OK. ... It’s all love. I still love everybody here and I’m looking forward to tomorrow.”
Dubón made a leaping catch over the left-field wall to rob Freeman of a home run in the third. Freeman wouldn't be denied an inning later. Hernández's homer to left drove in Andy Pages, who singled. One out later, Freeman pulled his 18th career postseason homer to right field for a 3-0 lead.
Lineup change
Roberts moved designated hitter Shohei Ohtani down to No. 5 in the lineup because Ohtani was 3 for 15 in his career against Sale. Ohtani went 0 for 4 with two strikeouts against Sale when the Dodgers lost 1-0 on Aug. 26 in Atlanta.
Roberts correctly predicted Ohtani would have opportunities with runners on base hitting lower in the order.
With runners on first and second in the first, Sale struck out Ohtani to end the inning. With two runners on base in the third, Ohtani reached on catcher's interference by Drake Baldwin to load the bases before Miguel Rojas ended the inning with a flyball to right field. Ohtani walked to lead off the eighth against Brent Suter, Atlanta's fourth pitcher.
Baldwin's bases-loaded grounder to first base drove in Dubón, who singled, in the fifth for Atlanta's only run.
Injury report
Rojas left during an at-bat in the eighth. The second baseman appeared to injure his back on a swing and was replaced by Tommy Edman. The Dodgers announced the injury as lower back pain.
Roberts said Rojas probably won't start on Wednesday and his availability off the bench will be determined before the game.
“I give him credit for conceding that at-bat,” Roberts said.
Weiss made a late change, moving Ronald Acuña Jr. from right field to designated hitter. Weiss said Acuña jammed his knee on a slide in Game 2. Acuña remained in the game but the knee was sore on Tuesday, leading to the lineup change.
Milestone win for Roberts
Roberts now has 71 career postseason wins, tying Tony La Russa for second-most in major league history. Joe Torre is first with 84.
Up next
Braves right-hander Tyler Mahle is expected to face Dodgers right-hander Tyler Glasnow in Game 4 on Wednesday night. Mahle said Tuesday an abdominal pull is now a “non-issue.” He felt the pull before allowing one run in seven innings of a 4-3 loss to Philadelphia in 10 innings during the NL Wild Card Series last week.
___

item.title: [MLB.com] Dubón le niega un jonrón a Freeman... pero Freddie cobra revancha después
item.dc:creator: Paul Casella
item.description: Después de que Sale consiguiera cada uno de sus primeros seis outs por la vía del ponche en el Juego 3 de la SDLN contra los Dodgers, Dubón registró el primer out defensivo y lo hizo de manera espectacular. Con un corredor en primera y nadie fuera en la parte alta del tercer inning, la exsuperestrella de los Bravos Freddie Freeman conectó un batazo profundo hacia el jardín izquierdo que salió de su bate a 101.3 mph. Dubón siguió la trayectoria de la pelota hasta la pared y calculó perfectamente
item.content:encoded:
Después de que Sale consiguiera cada uno de sus primeros seis outs por la vía del ponche en el Juego 3 de la SDLN contra los Dodgers, Dubón registró el primer out defensivo y lo hizo de manera espectacular.
Con un corredor en primera y nadie fuera en la parte alta del tercer inning, la exsuperestrella de los Bravos Freddie Freeman conectó un batazo profundo hacia el jardín izquierdo que salió de su bate a 101.3 mph. Dubón siguió la trayectoria de la pelota hasta la pared y calculó perfectamente su salto para realizar la atrapada justo frente a un grupo de relevistas de los Dodgers, quienes se preparaban para que la bola cayera en el bullpen de los visitantes.
La atrapada de Dubón probablemente le robó un posible jonrón de dos carreras a Freeman, pero como mínimo evitó un extrabase y, casi con toda seguridad, una carrera o dos en el episodio.
Los Dodgers llenaron las bases gracias a un sencillo de Will Smith con dos outs y a que Shohei Ohtani llegó a salvo por interferencia del receptor, pero Sale salió ileso al hacer que Miguel Rojas conectara una línea al jardín derecho para terminar la entrada.
Antes de siquiera necesitar la ayuda de su defensa, Sale se unió a Mike Hampton (Juego 2 de la SDLN del 2003) como los únicos lanzadores de los Bravos en conseguir cada uno de sus primeros seis outs por la vía del ponche en un juego de postemporada.
Freeman se desquitó en su siguiente turno al bate, cuando disparó con autoridad un cuadrangular hacia el jardín derecho-central, el 18vo vuelacercas de su carrera en postemporada, para darle a los Dodgers una ventaja de 3-0.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Dodgers beat Braves on Kiké Hernández and Freddie Freeman homers, take 2-1 NLDS lead

item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
ATLANTA — The Dodgers went into Game 3 of the National League Division Series knowing they couldn’t be so reliant on the home run, especially with Braves ace Chris Sale on the mound. And yet, in a 3-1 win, it was the home run ball, paired with a masterful performance on the mound from right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto, that secured the victory.
The Dodgers pulled ahead to a 2-1 lead in the best-of-five series.
The Dodgers tried to score in other ways, putting on six baserunners in the first three innings of the game. But it didn’t work.
They failed to take advantage of some luck and poor defense from the Braves in the first inning, as Mookie Betts beat out a soft ground ball up the first base line and Teoscar Hernández reached on a fielding error by Braves shortstop Ha-Seong Kim.
Yoshinobu gives up four hits and strikes out 10 and Kiké Hernández hits a two-run home run to power the Dodgers to victory in Game 3 of the NLDS.
The lineup shuffling manager Dave Roberts did against Sale had superstar Shohei Ohtani, batting fifth, walking up to the plate with two outs and runners on first and second. His over-anxious approach at the plate so far this postseason followed him into the at-bat. And he struck out whiffing on a slider in the opposite batter’s box.
The next inning, Kyle Tucker hit a two-out single into left, baited Sale into picking over to first base twice, and then stole second. But he was stranded there, as Kiké Hernández went down swinging. All six of the Dodgers’ outs in the first two innings came via the strikeout.
In the third, the Dodgers loaded the bases. Mookie Betts started the effort with a double through the left side of the infield. And it looked for a moment as if Freddie Freeman had capitalized on the opportunity with a runner in scoring position.
He stayed back on a fastball and crushed it to deep left field, on a trajectory to just clear the short fence. But Braves left fielder Mauricio Dubón made a leaping catch, holding into the ball as he slammed into the wall.
Undeterred, the Dodgers kept putting runners on base. With two outs, Will Smith stayed through a slider to single. Ohtani clipped Braves catcher Drake Baldwin’s mitt and was awarded first base for catcher’s interference. Then Miguel Rojas, who’d exit the game in the eighth inning mid-at-bat with what the Dodgers called low back pain, hit a line drive that found leather to end the inning.
So, back to the long ball.
Perennial postseason hero Kiké Hernández delivered the first blow. With Andy Pages on first, after his first hit of the series, Hernández launched a changeup into the left-field stands. Then, two batters later, Freeman turned on an inside sinker and sent it over the right-field fence — where Dubón had no chance to track it down.
Game 3 was billed as a matchup between aces: Sale, whom the Braves tabbed for Tuesday because of his workload in their wild-card series, and Yamamoto, whom the Dodgers partially held back for the first two games with the NLCS in mind.
Yamamoto held up his end of the bargain, limiting the Braves to four hits and one run in seven innings.
He retired 10 of the first 11 batters he faced. The only baserunner in that time, Michael Harris II, bunted for a single. Yamamoto crashed hard, slipping on the slick grass as he tried to pivot but still managing to make a throw to first from the ground.
Shohei Ohtani is batting fifth in the lineup against Braves ace Chris Sale in Game 3 of the NLDS. He hasn’t hit fifth or lower in a starting lineup since 2020 with the Angels.
He only wavered in the fifth, loading the bases with a pair of singles and a four-pitch walk. The Braves’ batting order turned over, and Yamamoto got Baldwin to ground out to first, but that allowed a run. Then he induced Ronald Acuña Jr. to ground out to second to escape the jam. Rojas ranged to his left to field the ball and made an on-target throw even as he slipped on the grass in shallow right field.
Yamamoto didn’t allow another baserunner.
Left-handed reliever Tanner Scott served as the Dodgers’ setup man, throwing a hitless eighth. And right-hander Edwin Díaz came in for his first save opportunity since Aug. 14 against the Brewers.
He gave up a double off the wall to Ozzie Albies to open the inning but retired the next three batters.

item.title: [New York Post] Dave Roberts proves he’s a playoff wizard again as Dodgers erupt in 4th inning against Braves
item.dc:creator: Thomas L Murray
item.description: Freddie Freeman and Kiké Hernández continue to add to their postseason résumés. But Hernandez needed to show off his bat first. Hernández saw an 89 MPH changeup come his way by Br
item.content:encoded:
Freddie Freeman and Kiké Hernández continue to add to their postseason résumés.
An inning after Freeman was denied an opposite-field home run over the left field wall at Truist Park by Mauricio Dubón, he thought he might try hitting one right.
But Hernandez needed to show off his bat first.
The two got the Dodgers on the board, to give them a 3-0 lead in the fourth inning of the NLDS, by hitting home runs over the walls in left and right field.
Hernández saw an 89 MPH changeup come his way by Braves starting pitcher Chris Sale and sent it 406 feet out of the park for a two-run homer. One batter later, Freeman obliterated a 96 MPH sinker and sent it screaming off the bat at 103 MPH for 399 feet.
Sale managed to get out of the inning in the following at-bat, but at first glance, it looked he was going to gve up another homer.
Teoscar Hernández just came short of Sale’s slider out of the park, after hard-hitting Sale at 108 MPH.
Both Freeman and Hernandez, continue to show why they are dominant in October, as both of them have had playoff heroics.
Freeman has a career batting average of .268 with 82 hits, 17 home runs, and 40 RBI through 81 postseason games.
Kiké Hernández has a career average of .272 with 80 hits and 16 home runs, with 42 RBIs in the postseason.
The combination of Hernández and Freeman came on the same day; manager Dave Roberts made a surprising decision to bump four-time MVP Shohei Ohtani down to the fifth hole in the Dodgers lineup and have Freeman hitting second, behind Mookie Betts, while Hernández was hitting ninth.
So far, his decision is paying off as Los Angeles holds a 3-1 lead against the Braves.

item.content:encoded:
When will Dodgers' Tarik Skubal pitch next in NLDS? Here's the latest update appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Los Angeles Dodgers are currently gearing up for Game 3 of their NLDS series against the Atlanta Braves on Tuesday afternoon on the road. The Dodgers are currently tied 1-1 with Atlanta after dropping a frustrating contest in Game 2 at home over the weekend.
The Dodgers won Game 1 of this series thanks in large part to a dominant pitching performance from ace Tarik Skubal, and now, the latest reporting has revealed when Skubal could be on the mound again for Los Angeles.
"Tarik Skubal throwing bullpen session in preparation for his next start…possibly Game 5," reported David Vassegh of AM 570 LA Sports on X, formerly Twitter.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Of course, if the Dodgers have their way, they'll win the next two games in Atlanta and avoid a Game 5 altogether, in which case Skubal would likely be the starter for Game 1 of the ensuing NLCS.
However, Los Angeles certainly has their work cut out for them in order to make that scenario a reality. Los Angeles' main hitters, headlined by Mookie Betts and Shohei Ohtani, have largely been dormant so far in this series, with the team mustering just two runs in Sunday's loss to Atlanta despite the Braves running out an all-bullpen lineup.
On Tuesday, Los Angeles will face off against the formidable Chris Sale, who is coming off a long rest after Walt Weiss opted not to rush him back in Game 2 in a gutsy move that ended up paying off.
The Dodgers will certainly want to see their bats come to life in Game 3 to retake control of the series.
Game 3 between the Dodgers and Braves is slated to get underway at 6:00 pm ET from Atlanta.
Related: Why Joe Davis isn't on broadcast for Fox's Dodgers-Braves NLDS Game 3
