item.title: [The Sporting Tribune] Glasnow delivers strong final tune-up despite Dodgers loss
item.dc:creator: Fredo Cervantes
item.description: LOS ANGELES — Tyler Glasnow walked off the mound Thursday night having done almost everything the Dodgers could have asked of him. The result, however, belonged to the Padres. Glasnow carried a no-hit bid into the sixth inning and struck out 11 over 6⅓ innings in his final tune-up before the postseason, but the Padres broke through late and held on to beat the Dodgers, 4-2, in the final home game of the 2026 regular season at Uniqlo Field at Dodger Stadium. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Tyler Glasnow walked off the mound Thursday night having done almost everything the Dodgers could have asked of him.
The result, however, belonged to the Padres.
Glasnow carried a no-hit bid into the sixth inning and struck out 11 over 6⅓ innings in his final tune-up before the postseason, but the Padres broke through late and held on to beat the Dodgers, 4-2, in the final home game of the 2026 regular season at Uniqlo Field at Dodger Stadium.
The Dodgers finished the night 97-62, having already secured a first-round bye earlier Thursday. The Padres, meanwhile, clinched a postseason berth and will play in a Wild Card Series.
And with the postseason bracket beginning to take shape, there is a very real possibility these two teams could be back here in nine days.
For six innings, though, Glasnow looked every bit like a pitcher the Dodgers will want leading their rotation into October.
Ethan Salas broke up the no-hitter with a one-out single in the sixth. Salas eventually scored on a sacrifice fly, and two more singles helped the Padres add to its lead.
Glasnow entered the inning with the Dodgers still searching for their first run. He left it with the Padres ahead.
His final line was as sharp as the circumstances allowed: 6⅓ innings, three hits, three runs, all earned, two walks and 11 strikeouts on 91 pitches, 58 for strikes.
“I feel like I'm in a pretty good rhythm right now, so it's perfect time to bring it in to the postseason,” Glasnow said afterward.
The 11 strikeouts came on 79 pitches before he returned for the seventh, and the outing offered another encouraging sign for a Dodgers rotation preparing for the most important games of the season.
The Dodgers had opportunities against the Padres but repeatedly failed to capitalize, stranding seven runners through the middle innings.
Mookie Betts, meanwhile, continued to do what he has done all season: reach base.
Betts reached safely in all four plate appearances, going 3-for-4 with a double, two singles and a walk.
Shohei Ohtani also collected two hits, including an RBI double in the ninth inning that brought the Dodgers within two runs. Ohtani's late hit gave the Dodgers one final spark, but the Padres closed the door to finish off the regular-season home finale.
Dave Roberts said he has liked what he has seen from Ohtani over the past two games.
“The last 2 nights, he’s looked great,” Roberts said.
The Dodgers' final home game also provided another encouraging glimpse of Edwin Díaz.
Díaz worked a scoreless ninth, allowing no hits and striking out two on just 11 pitches. Since returning from the injured list, he has thrown four scoreless innings, allowing one hit and one walk while striking out eight.
Over his last four appearances, opponents are 1-for-13 with eight strikeouts.
Díaz said his slider is in its best shape right now, a development that comes at an important time as he tries to earn a spot on the Dodgers' postseason roster.
“I'm trying just to do my job. I'm just gonna wanna put zeros when they give me the ball,” Díaz said. “I'm ready to pitch every day. I just want them to keep trusting me and keep giving me the ball just to show them I'm ready to pitch in the postseason.”
Roberts called Thursday Díaz's best performance of his four appearances since returning.
“This has been the best of the four,” Roberts said.
There are only three regular-season games remaining, but the Dodgers have already accomplished one of their primary objectives. The first-round bye is secured. The home schedule is finished. Now comes the final push toward October.
The loss also did little to concern Roberts about the Dodgers' record against winning teams during the second half.
“I don’t think so, I don’t put stock into it,” Roberts said. “Once you get to the postseason, it’s a different game.”
That is the challenge waiting for the Dodgers.
Thursday was less about the standings than it was about getting their pieces in place. Glasnow looked in rhythm. Díaz continued to build momentum. Ohtani looked sharp at the plate. Betts reached base four times.
The Padres, meanwhile, celebrated a postseason berth in the visiting clubhouse.
There is still baseball to be played before October arrives. But with the Dodgers holding a bye and the Padres headed for the Wild Card round, Thursday's matchup may have offered a preview of a game that matters much more.
“We’re gonna have an exciting postseason, so just ride with us,” Roberts said.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

25 Sep 2026, 10:55 GMT+10

(Photo credit: William Liang)
Dustin Harris drove in the go-ahead run in the sixth inning as the visiting San Diego Padres made franchise history with a 4-2 victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday to clinch a spot in the playoffs for a third consecutive season.
San Diego starter Nick Pivetta opened with 4 2/3 scoreless innings and four relievers finished off the victory as the Padres (89-70) celebrated a third straight playoff berth for the first time in franchise history. Yuki Matsui (4-1) earned the win with a scoreless inning and Mason Miller gave up a run with two outs in the ninth before securing his 38th save.
Austin Hays, Ethan Salas and Fernando Tatis Jr. added RBI singles in the seventh inning as San Diego won for the 15th time in its past 17 games. The Padres will open the playoffs in the wild-card round.
Tyler Glasnow took a no-hitter into the sixth inning for the Dodgers (97-62), who also secured their objective by clinching a spot in a National League Division Series matchup and the first-round bye that comes with it. Los Angeles sealed a top-two spot in the NL when the Cincinnati Reds defeated the Atlanta Braves earlier in the day.
Mookie Betts had three of the Dodgers' seven hits as he dropped to the No. 2 spot in the order for the first time in six games.
In his second game since returning from the injured list because of biceps discomfort, Shohei Ohtani moved back into the leadoff spot and went 2-for-5 with a two-out RBI double in the ninth. The Dodgers scored their first run in the eighth when Betts was awarded home plate on a balk by Adrian Morejon.
Pivetta kept his team in the game in giving up four hits with a walk and seven strikeouts while throwing 87 pitches in his final start of the regular season.
The Padres broke through against Glasnow in the sixth. Salas' one out single to center was San Diego's first hit of the game. Tatis followed with a single and Harris delivered a sacrifice fly to center for a 1-0 advantage.
San Diego chased Glasnow in the seventh with all three of the run-scoring hits in the inning coming against Justin Wrobleski. Glasnow was charged with three runs on three hits over his 6 1/3 innings with a season-high 11 strikeouts.
With a crowd of 53,027, the Dodgers passed the 4 million mark in attendance for the second consecutive season.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Dodgers clinch No. 2 seed and important playoff bye despite loss to Padres
item.dc:creator: Kevin Baxter
item.description: - Click here to listen to this article - - The Dodgers clinched the National League’s No. 2 seed and a first-round playoff bye, gaining five crucial days to rest a battered roster before their Oct. 3 NLDS opener. - The Dodgers lose to the San Diego Padres 4-2 and drop the three-game series despite Tyler Glasnow carrying a no-hitter into the sixth inning. - The Padres clinched a postseason berth as the Dodgers prepare for their final regular-season series in San Francisco after drawing more
item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- The Dodgers clinched the National League’s No. 2 seed and a first-round playoff bye, gaining five crucial days to rest a battered roster before their Oct. 3 NLDS opener.
- The Dodgers lose to the San Diego Padres 4-2 and drop the three-game series despite Tyler Glasnow carrying a no-hitter into the sixth inning.
- The Padres clinched a postseason berth as the Dodgers prepare for their final regular-season series in San Francisco after drawing more than 4 million fans to Dodger Stadium this season.
The Dodgers didn’t win Thursday. But they got something far more valuable before they even took the field for their 4-2 loss to the San Diego Padres.
With the Atlanta Braves’ loss to the Cincinnati Reds earlier in the day, the Dodgers clinched the second seed in the National League playoffs and the first-round bye that goes with it. That means the Dodgers will get five days off next week to prepare for their playoff opener, a godsend for a bruised and bloodied team that has stumbled to the finish of the regular season.
“I think we all know why it’s important,” first baseman Freddie Freeman said of the break. “There’s a lot of us kind of limping toward the end here, a lot of aches and pains this year.”
For the Padres (89-70), the victory was important because it clinched a wild-card berth and a franchise-record third consecutive trip to the postseason.
In addition to Freeman, who has been hobbled all month by a sore right knee, the Dodgers are rushing to get designated hitter Shohei Ohtani and closer Edwin Díaz healthy. Both had big games Thursday with Ohtani going two for five with a run batted in, the first time he’s had multiple hits or an RBI in more than a month. Díaz, meanwhile, pitched a perfect ninth, striking out two.
Other players also are getting healthy. Center fielder Andy Pages, who missed a month with a broken hand, returned to the lineup three days ago. Dalton Rushing, who is competing for a bench spot on the postseason roster, is expected to be activated off the injured list Friday. Left-hander Blake Snell, who came out of his last start nine days ago after just an inning, will make his final postseason tuneup Saturday.
All of them will benefit from some additional rest before their playoff opener, at Dodger Stadium, on Oct. 3.
And speaking of Dodger Stadium, the No. 2 playoff seed carries another important perk: the home-field advantage for the Division Series — and possibly the World Series, if the Dodgers make it that far. Home has certainly been an advantage for the Dodgers, who drew a sellout crowd of 53,027 Thursday, pushing the team’s total home attendance over 4 million for the second straight year.
“It’s more turning of the turnstiles than any venue in the world,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “The amazing thing is that it’s not just localized. It’s international. Everyone looks different at Dodger Stadium.
“It’s spectacular and our players certainly feed off of it.”
The Dodgers are one of five franchises in big-league history to draw more than 4 million fans in a season but just two others — the Toronto Blue Jays, from 1991-93, and the New York Yankees, in the final four years at old Yankee Stadium — did it in consecutive seasons.
And the Dodgers are the only team to do it since 2008. They also lead the majors in road attendance this season, having drawn 2.82 million, or 36,159 a game. For some fans, it’s hard to separate their support from the team’s success.
“A synergy exists between we the fans and the players,” said Charles Flores, an associate professor at Cal State L.A. and lifelong Dodgers fan who attended more than a dozen games this season. “One inspires the other.”
Russ Hoffman of Santa Clarita, a season-ticket holder for 40 years, agrees.
“The atmosphere created by drawing so many fans definitely contributes to their success,” he said. “Winning continuously drives the attendance and the current ownership has committed the assets to do that.”
That edge can be even bigger in the playoffs. The Dodgers lost just five of 16 postseason games at home — a .688 winning percentage — en route to World Series titles the last two years.
“During the playoffs, Dodger Stadium is a tough place to play because it’s 56,000 crazed fans yelling on every play,” said Stan Brooks, an award-winning film producer and longtime season-ticket holder. “The fans are so loud and the environment is so intense every night.”
The Dodgers (97-62) will finish the regular season with three games this weekend in San Francisco, where they will continue their preparation for the postseason.
In the final home game of the regular season Mookie Betts, dropped to second in the lineup with Ohtani’s return, went three for four with a walk, raising his average for September to .367, while Freeman had two hits for the third time in four games.
“I’m just encouraged with Shohei getting a couple hits, Mookie staying hot. That’s what it’s all about,” Freeman said. “Getting hot right now.
“That’s all we were looking forward to this last week is getting our guys back on the field.”
That didn’t add up to much offense Thursday, with the Dodgers stranding eight runners and going 0 for 8 with men in scoring position through eight innings. They avoided their first shutout of the season at home on Adrian Morejon’s balk in the eighth before Ohtani doubled in the second run with two outs in the ninth.
For the past 17 years, Chaz Perea and his four-person crew have been responsible for every bit of stadium landscaping that isn’t the field itself.
On the mound, Tyler Glasnow, who will be the Dodgers’ fourth starter in the postseason, was perfect through three innings. He walked Fernando Tatis Jr. on four pitches to start the fourth but didn’t allow another Padres batter to reach base until Ethan Salas singled with one out in the sixth.
That proved costly when Tatis singled on the next pitch, sending Salas to third, from where he scored on Dustin Harris’ sacrifice fly, putting the Padres ahead to stay.
Glasnow (5-2) got out of the inning by striking out Manny Machado, giving him a season-high 11 strikeouts and 21 in his last two starts. But San Diego then blew the game open in the seventh, chasing Glasnow and scoring three times off reliever Justin Wrobleski on run-scoring singles by Austin Hayes, Salas and Tatis.
Staff writer Maddie Lee contributed to this report.

item.title: [sandiegouniontribune.com] Padres beat Dodgers to clinch third straight postseason berth
item.dc:creator: Kevin Acee
item.description: LOS ANGELES — Finally, they are in. The Padres spent sizable portions of this season seemingly on the edge of collapse every few weeks before surging back into contention. So being no-hit for five innings and then suddenly building a sizable lead and then holding on in a frenzied finish to the game that clinched their playoff berth seemed about right. The Padres got their first hit and their first run in the sixth inning and scored three more times in the seventh before turning the game over to
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Finally, they are in.
The Padres spent sizable portions of this season seemingly on the edge of collapse every few weeks before surging back into contention.
So being no-hit for five innings and then suddenly building a sizable lead and then holding on in a frenzied finish to the game that clinched their playoff berth seemed about right.
The Padres got their first hit and their first run in the sixth inning and scored three more times in the seventh before turning the game over to the back end of their bullpen to preserve a 4-2 victory.
Their high-leverage relievers were the strength and the most consistent part of their team all season, so it was also fitting that Jason Adam, Adrian Morejón and Mason Miller strung together the final three innings to get the Padres into the playoffs for a third consecutive season.
It is the first time in team history the Padres have qualified for three consecutive postseasons and just the 10th time they will head to the playoffs in their 58 years of existence.
This was the second time in this three-year span that the Padres were spraying champagne in the visitors’ clubhouse at Dodger Stadium, the site of so many glum postgames over the years.
The Padres had reached base just once, on a walk, in five innings against Dodgers starter Tyler Glasnow.
Then, suddenly, they took a lead with the major contributions being a single by a rookie who joined them on Sept. 1 and a sacrifice fly by a journeyman who was called up on Aug. 24.
The Padres’ first hit of the night was Ethan Salas’ flare the other way and just over the left side of the infield with one out in the sixth inning.
Fernando Tatis Jr. followed with a single grounded through the right side that sent Salas to third base, and Dustin Harris then hit a fly ball to center field that put the Padres up 1-0.
Yuki Matsui, who had gotten the final out in the fifth inning, got the first two outs in the sixth before Jason Adam threw one pitch to get the third out.
A one-out double in the seventh inning by Jackson Merrill off Glasnow and a pinch-hit single by Austin Hays after lefty Justin Wrobleski entered the game extended the Padres’ lead, and two-out singles by Salas and Tatis extended it further.
Adam retired the first two batters in the seventh. Morejón got the final out that inning and allowed a run in the eighth. Miller’s 38th save was earned with a four-out ninth inning in which the Dodgers scored again.
After Tommy Edman reached base when he swung through a slider that bounced past Salas, Shohei Ohtani doubled Edman home before Mookie Betts grounded out.
Padres starter Nick Pivetta matched Glasnow where it mattered most — on the scoreboard — for as long as he could.
He was pulled after yielding a two-out single in the fifth inning, and Matsui surrendered a single to Freddie Freeman before striking out Teoscar Hernández.
The Dodgers found out before the game that they had clinched a first-round bye in the playoffs, so they are essentially playing out the season to stay in shape.
Exactly three years after the Padres clinched a playoff berth with a victory at Dodger Stadium, they were playing on Thursday for the right to continue playing.
They are now striving over the next three days for the right to host their best-of-three National League Wild Card Series.
They are in position to do so, a game ahead of the Cubs, who also clinched a playoff berth Thursday. Because the Cubs won the series between the teams, the Padres have to finish a game ahead of the Cubs in the standings in order to remain the No.4 seed.

item.content:encoded:
カブス2－1マーリンズ（24日、シカゴ）米大リーグ、カブスがマーリンズ戦に勝利し、2年連続のポストシーズン進出を決めた。その歓喜の一戦で、「PCA」ことピート・クローアームストロング外野手（24）が、史上7人目となる「40本塁打＆40盗塁」を達成した。
今季45本塁打を放っているPCAは、一回に四球で出塁し、鮮やかに今季40個目の盗塁を成功させた。偉業達成の瞬間、本拠地リグリー・フィールドのファンは総立ちとなり、大歓声で快挙を祝福した。
過去に「40－40」を達成したのは、1988年のホセ・カンセコ（アスレチックス＝42本塁打・40盗塁）、96年のバリー・ボンズ（ジャイアンツ＝42本塁打・40盗塁）、98年のアレックス・ロドリゲス（マリナーズ＝42本塁打・46盗塁）、2006年のアルフォンゾ・ソリアーノ（ナショナルズ＝46本塁打・41盗塁）、23年のロナルド・アクーニャ（ブレーブス＝41本塁打・73盗塁）、そして史上初の「50－50」（54本塁打・59盗塁）をマークした24年の大谷翔平（ドジャース）。
今季、PCAは大谷とナ・リーグMVP争いを繰り広げてきた。しかし、大谷に故障離脱があり、現状ではPCAの初受賞が確実視されている。PCAの今季の活躍はメジャーに大ブームを巻き起こしているものの、それでも大谷の「50－50」の金字塔には及ばず、いかに大谷の記録が次元を超越していたかも浮き彫りになる。
両親ともに俳優というカリフォルニア州出身のPCAは、名門ハーバード＝ウェストレイク高校を経て、20年ドラフト1巡目（全体19位）でメッツから指名を受けプロ入り。21年にカブスへ移籍し、抜群の身体能力で頭角を現した。走攻守がそろった中堅手として急成長し、明るい性格からファンに愛されている。
主力の日本コンビとの交流も深い。ともに主軸を担う鈴木誠也外野手（32）を兄貴分と慕い、今永昇太投手（33）の登板日には、先頭打者アーチなどで援護してきた。今永は「50－50とか、60－60とかもできるのが彼のすごいところ」と賛辞を贈った。

item.title: [whittierdailynews.com] Dodgers’ Dalton Rushing to get brief audition for postseason spot
item.dc:creator: Doug Padilla
item.description: LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers will activate Dalton Rushing on Friday before their final regular-season series, giving the left-handed power hitter at least a few more days and a handful of at-bats to unleash his swing. The Dodgers are not ruling out a possible spot on a playoff roster, but as of now, they are just focused on giving Rushing the chance to take a few swings in San Francisco in a sign of respect. “At the most it would be three pinch-hit at-bats, so just conduct at-bats and see what you
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers will activate Dalton Rushing on Friday before their final regular-season series, giving the left-handed power hitter at least a few more days and a handful of at-bats to unleash his swing.
The Dodgers are not ruling out a possible spot on a playoff roster, but as of now, they are just focused on giving Rushing the chance to take a few swings in San Francisco in a sign of respect.
“At the most it would be three pinch-hit at-bats, so just conduct at-bats and see what you got,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “Just the circumstances of his situation, it’s just tough to just be hurt, come back, then be hurt again, and then take three pinch-hit at-bats to potentially then say, ‘Hey, you’re on the roster.’
“What he’s done for us this season certainly deserves some (playoff) consideration. That’s kind of giving him the respect and thoughtfulness of what he’s done for us.”
Rushing understands the situation and is fully on board with whatever decision is made.
His season was put in jeopardy when he went on the injured list in early August with an elbow injury that was diagnosed as a small UCL tear with a forearm flexor strain.
Determined to return as both a hitter and a catcher, Rushing worked at both sides of his game and returned on Sept. 1. But the continued throwing work outside of games led to a setback and he went back on the IL less than a week later.
“The at-bat’s really are the only side that I can truly help them in,” Rushing said Thursday. “Even then, it’s just a pinch-hit opportunity and no defense included, so I know that ties their hands up a little bit. But yeah, I’m excited.”
Without much time to make an impact, and the Dodgers also having the option of using left-handed-hitting rookie Josue De Paula on the playoff roster, Rushing is well aware of what he is up against. The club even has the option of using the lefty hitting Hyeseong Kim in the playoffs for his defense and speed.
“No hard feelings on either end,” Rushing said about getting a chance to play in the playoffs. “Obviously you want to play baseball. You feel healthy again to an extent. You feel healthy swinging a bat, so yeah, I want to get back soon.”
The next challenge is determining the extent of his elbow injury. Rushing is swinging pain-free after a platelet-rich plasma injection, but figuring out when he can throw again remains in question.
He is determined to rehab the injury, knowing that some kind of surgical procedure might be needed.
“I think as soon as we get into the offseason, that’s decision time,” Rushing said. “Progressing the way that I’m progressing right now, I’m very optimistic it is going to be totally fine and just think it was a lot of workload increase very quickly. I think that’s what sparked it. Once I got the shot, it felt really, really good.”
Roberts did not say what the full roster move will be on Friday.
VIEW FROM THE TOP
Shohei Ohtani was back in the leadoff spot on Thursday after batting second in his return from the IL on Wednesday.
While his turn as a No. 2 hitter came because the San Diego Padres had left-hander Robbie Ray on the mound, Roberts has not said if batting second against a lefty will be a regular feature of the lineup.
“I’m kind of toying with it clearly,” Roberts said. “But I’m not sure exactly whether he’s going to stick in the one or rotate him depending on the pitcher.”
Ohtani went 1 for 4 with a walk on Wednesday, but the comfort level he showed at the plate pleased Roberts.
“I hope that’s a sign of things to come,” Roberts said. “Taking the first slider from Robbie Ray for a ball, (that) got him into a good count, whereas the last couple weeks he was just hair-on-fire swinging and chasing. It’s a hard way to make a living that way, right? I thought (Wednesday) the patience was really good. I hope that’s more to come.”
CATCHING ON FAST
After starting the first two games of the series against the Padres, catcher Will Smith gave way to backup Hunter Feduccia on Thursday but was available off the bench.
Smith is also set to start two of the three games in San Francisco over the weekend before settling into an everyday role in the playoffs.
In the last five games Smith started, he was batting .421 (8 for 19) with three home runs and five RBIs. Since returning from neck inflammation on Sept. 1, he is batting .255 with four home runs and 11 RBIs in 19 games.
UP NEXT
Dodgers (LHP Tarik Skubal, 11-7, 2.85 ERA) at Giants (RHP Yunior Marte, 0-1, 4.66 ERA), Friday, 7:15 p.m., SportsNet LA, 570 AM, 1020 AM

item.description: ドジャース2－4パドレス（24日、ロサンゼルス）米大リーグ、ドジャースの大谷翔平投手（32）がパドレス戦に「1番・DH」で出場し、5打数2安打1打点。ノーアーチはドジャース移籍後ワーストを更新する15試合74打席となった。チームは敗れ、ポストシーズンの第2シードが確定した。 大谷は一回、先頭で右中間フェンス際に382フィート（約116.4メートル）の放物線を放つも中飛に倒れた。三回2死では右前打を放ち、復帰戦から2試合連続安打。五回も中堅深くに372フィート（約113.3メートル）の打球を放ったが、中飛に倒れた。七回は空振り三振、九回2死の第5打席は左中間に適時二塁打で復帰後初の長打とした。 ポストシーズン（PS）のシード権争いでは、ブレーブスがレッズに敗れ、ドジャースの第2シード以上が確定。また、ブルワーズが勝利し、ドジャースが敗れたため、ブルワーズの第1シードが確定、ドジャースは第2シードが確定となった。第1、2シードはワイルドカードシリーズが免除され、バイウイーク（休養週間）を獲得。地区シリーズ本拠地開催でPSの初戦を迎える。

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers lost 5-1 on Wednesday night in the second game of their series against the San Diego Padres.
This now sets up a rubber match on Thursday night between the two teams, as L.A. took Game 1 of the series back on Tuesday.
Ahead of the game, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts elected to make some moves near the top of his batting order following the return of Shohei Ohtani this week.
Dodgers Announce Mookie Betts Move
Since Ohtani's return, Roberts has placed him in the two-hole, batting behind leadoff hitter Mookie Betts.
Pretty much all season, hitting in the leadoff spot has been Ohtani's role, and he's excelled at it.
Ultimately, Betts has as well, but Roberts decided to make the switch back, and for the series finale, Ohtani will hit leadoff while Betts will drop down to the two-hole.
Here's the full Dodgers lineup:
Via Underdog MLB: "Dodgers 9/24 S. Ohtani DH M. Betts SS F. Freeman 1B T. Hernández LF K. Tucker RF M. Muncy 3B A. Pages CF H. Feduccia C T. Edman 2B T. Glasnow SP."
Looking at Betts' 2026 Season
In his 13th MLB season and seventh as a member of the Dodgers, it's been a challenging 2026 campaign at times, which he recently acknowledged.
"Thank you for sticking with me. I know it was hard. I make it hard sometimes, but thank you for sticking by my side. By our side. We've got something special coming," Betts said after clinching the playoffs.
Despite the highs and lows, Betts still had a pretty productive year by most standards. He's appeared in 119 games entering Thursday and has logged 464 at-bats, hitting .256 with 69 runs, 119 hits, 22 home runs, and 68 RBIs while slugging .450 with a .775 OPS.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Los Angeles Dodgers Announce Mookie Betts Move During Padres Series appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [MLB.com] Rushing to return for final series. Is that enough time to earn postseason spot?
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- As the Dodgers mull over how to assemble their postseason bench, part of the decision may come down to weighing one small sample of plate appearances against another.
The Dodgers plan to activate Dalton Rushing from the 10-day injured list before Friday's series opener against the Giants at Oracle Park, manager Dave Roberts said Thursday. Rushing, who will only be available as a hitter due to a partial tear of the ulnar collateral ligament in his right elbow, is expected to get three pinch-hit appearances at most during the final weekend of the regular season.
Rushing has taken just eight plate appearances since the beginning of August, when he sustained the elbow injury. He spent most of August on the IL, returned when rosters expanded on Sept. 1 and went back on the IL shortly afterward when he aggravated his elbow while working through a throwing progression.
It would be an uphill battle for Rushing to make the postseason roster, Roberts acknowledged. But the Dodgers want to give the 25-year-old backstop the chance to end the season with the big league club.
"Just the circumstances of his situation, it's just tough to just be hurt, be back, then be hurt again," Roberts said. "And then take three pinch-hit at-bats, potentially, and then say, 'Hey, you're on the roster.'
"What he's done for us this season certainly deserves some consideration. That's kind of giving him the respect and thoughtfulness of what he's done for us."
The likely front-runner to be the primary left-handed bat off the bench is top prospect Josue De Paula, who was optioned to Triple-A Oklahoma City when Shohei Ohtani was activated from the 15-day IL on Wednesday. De Paula's career in the big leagues spans a mere 11 games and 42 plate appearances -- but he greatly impressed the Dodgers with his ability to conduct an at-bat, hitting 10-for-31 (.323) and reaching base at a .500 clip.
"He's done everything he can to put himself in a position to be in the conversation for us as we're making our postseason roster," president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said.
Rushing has hardly played in the past two months, but he has a larger sample of big league plate appearances to draw on. He took a step forward in his second season in the Majors, hitting .249 with a .798 OPS and 12 homers.
So the Dodgers aren't only considering Rushing's next three plate appearances as they evaluate him for a potential bench role.
"It's a small track record, but it's a good track record," Roberts said.
Whether Rushing or De Paula best suits the Dodgers' bench needs is a more complex question. Both are essentially hitters only, Rushing due to his elbow and De Paula because his defense is a work in progress. De Paula would be a better option to run off the bench, as he swiped 30 bags in back-to-back Minor League seasons, while Rushing has never stolen more than two bases in a single professional season.
But if the Dodgers really wanted to round out their bench with a designated runner or defensive specialist, then carrying someone like Hyeseong Kim would make more sense than either Rushing or De Paula. Roberts said that he could see the team carrying 14 position players and 12 pitchers in the best-of-five NL Division Series -- opening an additional spot on the bench -- whereas in the best-of-seven NL Championship Series, the team would probably lean toward carrying the maximum 13 pitchers.
So while performance at the big league level matters, the decision will be more involved for Rushing, De Paula and the Dodgers' other postseason bench options.
"There's some nuanced conversation that needs to happen," Roberts said, "and what fits best for a potential first-round matchup."

item.content:encoded:
Vuelve la estrella de Dodgers: Shohei Ohtani sale de la lista de lesionados a días de los playoffs
El astro japonés vuelve al orden al bate frente a los Padres tras superar molestias físicas; aunque Dave Roberts descartó que lance este año, los Dodgers confían en su bate para buscar el tricampeonato.
Shohei Ohtani regresará este miércoles a la alineación de Dodgers en el segundo juego de la serie contra Padres, después de pasar 15 días en la lista de lesionados tras sufrir molestias en su bíceps derecho y rodilla izquierda.
La ausencia de la estrella de Dodgers fue programada para encarar la última semana de la campaña regular y tomar ritmo para la postemporada, que inicia la semana entrante.
Con cinco juegos restantes en la temporada regular, Ohtani no alcanzará los 611 turnos que tomó el año pasado, pues acumula 502.
Te puede interesar: Padres vs Dodgers hoy: dónde ver EN VIVO el regreso de Ohtani tras 15 días en la lista de lesionado
Menos turnos y producción ofensiva
Las ausencias en el plato también han repercutido en su línea de bateo, con 55 jonrones, 25 menos que la campaña anterior, así como 80 carreras remolcadas, 22 menos en comparación con 2025, cuando registró 102.
La ausencia reciente de 15 días es la más extensa para el japonés desde que, en 2023, jugando para Angelinos, se perdió 25 juegos por problemas en el oblicuo y codo.
En el primero de los diez años de contrato con Dodgers, en 2024, el japonés solo fungió como bateador designado, pues se recuperaba de una segunda operación en su codo derecho.
Ohtani no volverá al montículo este año
Dave Roberts, mánager de Dodgers, ya había revelado que el japonés no formaría parte de la rotación de lanzadores en lo que resta de la temporada, incluyendo los playoffs.
Sin embargo, esperan que Ohtani sea clave en la ofensiva durante la postemporada, pues el año pasado pegó ocho jonrones en 16 juegos rumbo al campeonato de la Serie Mundial.
Dodgers se mantiene como el segundo mejor equipo de la Liga Nacional (96-60), a dos juegos de los Cerveceros (98-58), quienes le ganaron la serie anual, por lo que tendrán a su favor el criterio de desempate.
Dodgers también buscan ser el primer tricampeón desde que Yankees lo hizo entre 1998 y 2000.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers already step closer to World Series three-peat, even before playoffs begin
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: The Dodgers are already another step closer to a third straight World Series. Thanks to the Braves’ loss to the Reds on Thursday night, the Dodgers were assured of finishing the season with a top-two record in the National League, clinching a first-round bye that ensures they will not be subjected to a best-of-three wild-card series next week. item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers are already another step closer to a third straight World Series.
Thanks to the Braves’ loss to the Reds on Thursday night, the Dodgers were assured of finishing the season with a top-two record in the National League, clinching a first-round bye that ensures they will not be subjected to a best-of-three wild-card series next week.
Instead, the Dodgers will begin their postseason quest in the National League Division Series at Dodger Stadium on Saturday, Oct. 3, holding home-field advantage for that best-of-five series as they go for the first three-peat by an NL team in MLB history.
First-round byes have not always been kind to the Dodgers.
After MLB expanded its postseason field five years ago — creating a five-day layoff for the top-two seeds in each league between the end of the regular season and the start of their playoff schedules — the Dodgers were knocked out in the NLDS as a bye team in 2022 and 2023. Both years, questions about the negative side effects of the weeklong break loomed large in the wake of their elimination.
Thus, after receiving a bye again in 2024, the team altered its off-week schedule, incorporating more simulated game activities and making a concerted effort to spend more time at the ballpark together on workout days.
It paid off in that year’s division series, when the Dodgers overcame a two-games-to-one deficit to the Padres en route to the first of their back-to-back titles.
Last year, the team failed to earn a top-two seed but swept the Reds in two games in the wild-card series to begin their World Series defense.
This season, securing a bye became a critical objective for the club down the stretch. The last thing their aging roster needed was two extra playoff games. Ongoing injuries to Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman also amplified the importance of getting extra time off ahead of another October gauntlet.
“It’s always helpful in the sense of giving your guys a break to reset,” manager Dave Roberts said earlier this month. “But given all the tax and where our guys are healthwise, to get that week would be huge.”
The Dodgers, who entered Thursday with a 97-61 record, still have an outside shot at the NL’s No. 1 seed, as well, but would need to run the table over the season’s final weekend and have the Brewers — who currently hold MLB’s best record at 100-59 — get swept in their final series against the already-eliminated Cardinals.
“I think it’s more about just playing good baseball,” Roberts said this week when asked how much of a priority the top seed would be. “The last couple weeks, we’ve just played good baseball, and the fallout is this or that. We want to get the bye, and then if it happens that we keep playing well and we gain a couple games on the Brewers, great.”
Indeed, the club’s primary postseason seeding objectives have already been met. They’ve won their 13th NL West division title in the last 14 years. They’ve given themselves the shortest possible route through the playoffs. And now, they’ll have ample time next week to prepare for an unprecedented three-peat bid.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dave Roberts Mulls Changes as Dodgers Finish Home Schedule
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb

With Shohei Ohtani back in the lineup, several key hitters finding their swings and Tyler Glasnow taking the mound for the final regular-season home game, the Dodgers have plenty to feel good about despite Wednesday’s loss to the Padres. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers will get another opportunity to secure a first-round postseason bye Thursday night, and manager Dave Roberts likes what he’s seeing from his team as October approaches. With Shohei Ohtani back in the lineup, several key hitters finding their swings and Tyler Glasnow taking the mound for the final regular-season home game, the Dodgers have plenty to feel good about despite Wednesday’s loss to the Padres.
Speaking with reporters before the game, Roberts discussed Ohtani’s encouraging return, the offensive resurgence of Kyle Tucker and Teoscar Hernández, the difficult postseason roster decisions ahead and the possibility of another meeting with San Diego in October.
One of the nuggets that Doc floated in his pregamer was the possibility of not necessarily hitting Shohei Ohtani in the leadoff spot throughou the playoffs. He might, as he did on Wednesday, use Mookie Betts in the leadoff spot on nights when the opponents throw a lefty at them.
Ohtani’s Presence Changes Everything
Roberts was asked whether a single position player can have the kind of impact in baseball that a quarterback has in football or a superstar has in basketball.
He believes Ohtani is one of the rare players capable of doing exactly that.
“Yes, he can have an impact. Certainly, the biggest impact in baseball is the starting pitcher, I believe. But as far as Shohei, what he can do in the batter’s box can certainly make that impact.”
“Every time he steps in the box, he can change the score. And when he’s in the hole, when he’s on deck, he’s always looming. That plays into the pitcher’s mind, psyche, the manager, the pitching coach.”
Roberts was particularly encouraged by Ohtani’s plate discipline Wednesday, when he went 1-for-4 with a walk and narrowly missed a home run on a seventh-inning fly ball to center field.
“I hope that’s a sign of things to come,” Roberts said. “I thought even yesterday, taking the first slider from Robbie Ray for a ball got him into a good count. Whereas the last couple weeks, just really hair-on-fire swinging and chasing. It’s a hard way to make a living that way, right?”
“I thought yesterday the patience was really good. And like I said, I hope that’s more to come.”
The manager reiterated that he wants Ohtani to control the strike zone and use the big part of the field.
“If he can do those things, then sign me up.”
As for where Ohtani will hit in the batting order going forward, Roberts is still considering his options.
“I haven’t totally decided. I’m kind of toying with it, clearly. I’m not sure exactly whether he’s going to stick in the one or rotate him depending on the pitcher. Not totally 100% yet.”
Dodgers Offense Finding Its Stride
The Dodgers managed only one run Wednesday despite collecting 10 hits, but Roberts believes the overall quality of their offensive approach has improved considerably.
Asked how he feels about the lineup compared with a month ago, particularly with Mookie Betts, Tucker and Hernández swinging the bats well, Roberts offered an enthusiastic assessment.
“I feel much better about our offense now,” he said. “We didn’t score a bunch of runs last night, but I thought how we beat the starter was a good start. And we’ve done it the last two nights.”
“It’s just a relentless lineup. You can kind of stagger them left, right, all the way one through nine. There’s no easy outs. There’s a lot of guys that can slug you. We control the strike zone.”
The simultaneous resurgence of several hitters is especially encouraging.
“Now you get Kyle getting some hits. You get Teo slugging, getting some hits, and all the while taking his walks, too.”
“This is the most we’ve had guys that are swinging the bats at the same time all year. It’s probably five guys that feel really good right now, where typically it’s one or two. So this is a good thing.”
That’s certainly a welcome development with the postseason just around the corner.
Dalton Rushing Expected Back Friday, but October Roster Remains Uncertain
Roberts confirmed that Dalton Rushing is expected to be activated Friday, although his opportunity to demonstrate his readiness for the postseason will be extremely limited.
“It’s going to be a small sample,” Roberts acknowledged. “At the most, it would be three pinch-hit at-bats. So just conduct good at-bats and see what we got.”
The manager expressed sympathy for Rushing’s difficult circumstances, particularly after dealing with multiple injuries.
“It’s just tough to be hurt, be back, then to be hurt again, and then to take three pinch-hit at-bats potentially and say, ‘Hey, you’re on the roster.'”
“But what he’s done for us this year certainly deserves some consideration. I think that’s giving him the respect and the thoughtfulness of what he’s done for us.”
Roberts also explained that the Dodgers must consider more than simply adding another left-handed bat. Bench versatility and the potential need for a pinch-runner will factor into the final decision.
“There’s also a component of having a guy that can run off the bench. So it’s not just a left-handed bat off the bench. There are some other nuanced conversations that need to happen, and what fits best for a potential first-round matchup.”
He added that a five-game Division Series creates different pitching requirements than a longer Championship Series, potentially giving the Dodgers more flexibility with their bench construction.
Glasnow Gets One More Tune-Up
Thursday’s starter, Tyler Glasnow, will make his sixth appearance since returning from the injured list.
Roberts expressed satisfaction with the right-hander’s progress, particularly his delivery and how he’s managing his outings.
“I’ve seen that he hasn’t really had concerns about the delivery. I think the ball’s coming out really well.”
“I like some of the things that he gets frustrated about versus years past. I think he’s just managing his outings really well.”
Although Roberts wants Glasnow to finish the regular season on a positive note, he emphasized that Thursday’s performance won’t determine how he views the pitcher’s postseason readiness.
“This is going to be a good one, obviously, for the confidence to go into the postseason. But either way, it’s not make or break. I just want him to pitch well and feel good going into October.”
A Potential October Preview
Roberts acknowledged that the Dodgers are paying close attention to the Padres during this final regular-season series, recognizing that the two clubs could meet again in the playoffs.
He mentioned gathering information on Robbie Ray, Michael King and San Diego’s bullpen, with Nick Pivetta scheduled to pitch Thursday.
The Dodgers are also keeping an eye on the Braves, whose result against Cincinnati could affect Los Angeles’ opportunity to clinch the bye.
But Roberts said a favorable result on the out-of-town scoreboard wouldn’t change his approach in the middle of Thursday’s game.
“We’re playing to win, and I don’t think if the scoreboard reads that they’re winning or they lost, it would change anything.”
“I want to win tonight.”
Four Million Reasons to Celebrate Dodger Baseball
Thursday’s home finale also comes with a significant milestone, as the Dodgers are expected to surpass four million in attendance for the second consecutive season.
Roberts praised the organization’s ability to draw fans from around the world and the atmosphere they create at Dodger Stadium.
“The amazing thing is that it’s not just localized, clearly. It’s not just domestic. It’s international. You look at everyone, everyone looks different in Dodger Stadium. It’s spectacular, and our players certainly feed off of it.”
“It’s not taken for granted. I think opponents feel it, certainly in the later innings, when they see the third deck full and the speakers are blaring.”
Roberts credited the organization’s ownership and front office for consistently putting a star-studded team on the field.
“Los Angeles loves stars, and they want to see superstars, and we have a lot of superstars, which draws people. And I think our product is very consistent.”
For a team preparing for its 14th consecutive postseason appearance, Thursday offers another opportunity to reward those fans with something worth celebrating.
The Dodgers have already clinched the NL West. Now they can secure the first-round bye, give their pitching staff some much-needed rest and head into October with their biggest stars appearing to find their form at precisely the right time.

A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Top Prospect Josue De Paula Could Still Play a Role for the Dodgers in 2026
item.dc:creator: Justin Binkowski

item.content:encoded:
Outfielder Josue De Paula's first stint with the Los Angeles Dodgers has officially come to a close. But that doesn't necessarily mean he won't wear a Dodgers uniform again this year.
De Paula, MLB Pipeline's No. 6 overall prospect for 2026, was optioned to Triple-A on Wednesday as the Dodgers activated two-way star Shohei Ohtani from the injured list. The 21-year-old made his MLB debut on Sept. 11 and appeared in 11 games for Los Angeles, hitting .323 (10-for-31) with one home run, seven RBIs, seven runs scored, and 11 walks.
Most notably, De Paula was promoted to the big leagues straight from Double-A. So, with this recent roster move, the young prospect made his Triple-A debut on Wednesday in the Oklahoma City Comets' playoff game. The 6-foot-3 outfielder went 0-for-3 with two walks and a run scored in Oklahoma City's 7-2 postseason victory over the Las Vegas Aviators, the Athletics' Triple-A affiliate. But this might not be the only taste of playoff baseball the lefty-swinging slugger gets in 2026.
Will the Dodgers actually consider putting Josue De Paula on their playoff roster?
Although De Paula was optioned on Wednesday, he's still eligible for the Dodgers' National League Division Series roster, according to The Athletic's Fabian Ardaya. Ardaya said the young outfielder could "be given heavy consideration" for a spot on the postseason team, but it remains to be seen whether Los Angeles will go down that route.
While his first stint in the majors was brief, De Paula regularly showcased his offensive skill set and ability to get on base. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts even called him a "special hitter," according to Ardaya. But Los Angeles mostly used the 21-year-old as a designated hitter, limiting him to two games in the big-league outfield. And now that Ohtani is back, the Dodgers don't have an immediate need for a DH.
As things stand, it's unclear if De Paula will be on Los Angeles' postseason roster. If he is included, it'll most likely be in a pinch-hit role, unless an injury pops up. Either way, the talented prospect has quickly shown that he can make an impact for the Dodgers now and in the future.
Justin Binkowski is a lifelong baseball fan returning to cover the sport he loves after spending nearly a decade writing about video games. Before his time as managing editor at Dot Esports, Binkowski attended King's College in Wilkes-Barre, PA, where he was also a relief pitcher on the school's baseball team. While in college, Binkowski was a media relations intern for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders during the 2014 season.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Dave Roberts Announces Dalton Rushing News Ahead of Dodgers vs Padres Series Finale
item.dc:creator: Noah Camras; Unknown
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers will give Dalton Rushing three games — and that likely means, at most, three at-bats — to prove he's worth a spot on the team's postseason roster. Manager Dave Roberts announced before Thursday's series finale with the San Diego Padres that Rushing will be activated off the injured list ahead of Friday's game against the San Francisco Giants. With that activation, Rushing will have just three games to play in before the season ends. Since he's unable to catch, he's merely
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers will give Dalton Rushing three games — and that likely means, at most, three at-bats — to prove he's worth a spot on the team's postseason roster.
Manager Dave Roberts announced before Thursday's series finale with the San Diego Padres that Rushing will be activated off the injured list ahead of Friday's game against the San Francisco Giants.
With that activation, Rushing will have just three games to play in before the season ends. Since he's unable to catch, he's merely a pinch-hit option off the bench, which is the role he'd play for the team in October.
While Rushing could theoretically be the Dodgers' designated hitter, they just got Shohei Ohtani back, and want him to get as many at-bats as possible before the postseason begins.
Thus, Rushing will likely have a maximum of three plate appearances as a pinch hitter over the final three games of the season to make his case.
It appears Rushing is battling with top prospect Josue De Paula — who was optioned on Wednesday but remains eligible to return before the National League Division Series — for a spot on the postseason roster.
Roberts admitted earlier this week that Rushing likely has the tougher path to winning the spot.
“Hitting off the bench is very difficult and so you're just trying to figure out who gives us the best chance," Roberts said. “To be quite frank, it’s going to be tougher for Dalton given the time that he’s missed, and to kind of think that you have three games to get back in the playoff form, which is tough to do. It’s not a knock on him. He’s been great for us. but it’s still tough given that also you’re talking about the consistency of at-bats recently from Josue.
“We have to have those conversations and make a decision.”
Roberts said on Thursday that the team wanted to give Rushing one more opportunity after everything he did for the team this year. He stepped into a starting role amid Will Smith's extended absence, and hit .249 across 78 games with 12 home runs, 36 RBIs and an OPS of .798.
Rushing said to the LA Times that he's hoping to be able to impact the team in any way come October.
“Just showing them that I can swing it, and it’s an option,” Rushing said. “I know that you kind of tie [the team’s] hands up when you can’t play defense. So, I’m not expecting anything… just continue to take at-bats and see where we go from there.”

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers and San Diego Padres are facing off in the rubber match of their three-game series on Thursday night with plenty at stake for both teams.
The Dodgers, who have already won the National League West division, can clinch a first-round bye with a win or Atlanta Braves loss over the season's final four games.
They're also still chasing the Milwaukee Brewers for the No. 1 seed, but will need some help to secure home-field advantage throughout the postseason.
As for the Padres, they're looking to clinch a postseason spot, with their magic number currently sitting at 1.
Thus, the winner of Thursday's game will be celebrating in some capacity. If it's the Padres, they'll be making a champagne and beer mess in the visitor's clubhouse at Dodger Stadium. If it's the Dodgers, they'll be shaking hands and looking forward to their five-day layoff beginning next week.
Dodgers vs Padres Pitching Matchup on Thursday
Right-handed pitcher Tyler Glasnow is taking the mound for the Dodgers in his final tune-up before the postseason.
Glasnow has been shaky since coming off the injured list at the end of August, sporting a 4.50 ERA over 28 innings with 38 strikeouts to 10 walks. Overall this season, he's 5-1 with a 3.46 ERA and 87 strikeouts across 67.2 innings (12 starts).
Glasnow is expected to be the team's No. 4 starter in the playoffs behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell.
Opposite Glasnow will be Padres right-hander Nick Pivetta, who missed nearly five months this season with an elbow injury but has been incredibly sharp since returning.
In his three starts since coming off the IL, Pivetta has allowed just three runs over 14 innings for a 1.93 ERA. He has 11 strikeouts to one walk in that time.
Dodgers Starting Lineup
- Shohei Ohtani, DH
- Mookie Betts, SS
- Freddie Freeman, 1B
- Teoscar Hernández, LF
- Kyle Tucker, RF
- Max Muncy, 3B
- Andy Pages, CF
- Hunter Feduccia, C
- Tommy Edman, 2B
How to Watch Dodgers vs Padres on Thursday
First pitch for Los Angeles Dodgers vs. San Diego Padres on Thursday, Sept. 24 is 7:10 p.m. PT/10:10 p.m. ET.
The game will be broadcast on SportsNet LA and in the MLB app.
The game will be broadcast on the radio on AM570 (in English) and KTNQ 1020 AM (in Spanish).

item.title: [sgvtribune.com] Alexander: Wouldn’t another Dodgers-Padres playoff series be fun?
item.dc:creator: Jim Alexander

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — If there are any messages being sent this week, they’re subtle ones.
The Dodgers and Padres have become quite the rivalry in recent years. The Padres’ stars, particularly Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado, get on the nerves of Dodger fans. San Diegans, with their tendency to dislike all things associated with the metropolis to the north – except for that segment of folks who still can’t totally let go of the Chargers – relish the opportunity to, well, beat L.A.
Consider: When the Padres finally slew the dragon from the north as the late Peter Seidler, then owner, memorably predicted, they did everything but push back closing time in the Gaslamp Quarter. The roar that accompanied that 2022 National League Division Series victory might still be echoing in Petco Park all these years later, so hungry were Padres fans to take down the Dodgers, especially after L.A. had beaten them on neutral ground in the 2020 COVID-19-influenced postseason.
It’s also fairly obvious that the Dodgers’ 2022 failure, followed by a 2023 NLDS sweep by the Arizona Diamondbacks, helped create the monster in Chavez Ravine that is currently terrorizing all of baseball, including the segment of ownership that is willing to push the game to the brink in its zeal for a salary cap that labor has no intention of ever accepting.
You think Andrew Friedman and the rest of the Dodgers’ front office didn’t redouble their efforts following those two playoff flameouts? The mere possibility of a three-peat now should be proof of how much those losses stung. And the hype video in Dodger Stadium these nights is a pretty accurate representation of the state of mind here, the feeling that the Dodgers and their fans not only don’t care that they’ve become baseball’s villains, they relish it.
As the voiceover narrator puts it, “What’s wrong with being the bad guy? If being the best makes you bad, so be it. … If we’re being honest, sometimes it’s fun to root for the bad guy. … You need teams like us so you can point your finger and say, ‘That’s the bad guy.’”
The villainy works both ways, of course. Witness the first inning of the first game of this current series on Tuesday night.
Machado provokes strong reactions in L.A. because (a) he spent the final months of the 2018 season with the Dodgers, (b) his style of play was, shall we say, overly energy efficient – or, as he put it, “I’m not the type of player that’s going to be ‘Johnny Hustle’” – and (c) after that season he signed a 10-year, $300 million free agent contract with San Diego.
So, in Game 1 on Tuesday night, Brock Stewart’s first pitch to Machado knocked him down. The crowd jeered, loudly, and Machado took the moment to sit there and nod his head as if to say, “Yeah, it’s on.”
There were no further dust-ups in the first two games of this series, a 7-0 Dodgers victory on Tuesday night and a 5-1 Padres victory on Wednesday.
This wasn’t quite on the order of the series in June 2025, when then-Padres manager Mike Shildt and Dodgers outfielder Andy Pages exchanged words on the first night after Pages was hit by a pitch, Tatis and Shohei Ohtani were both plunked and Dodgers manager Dave Roberts was eventually ejected the second night, and Roberts and Shildt exchanged words at home plate after Tatis was hit again in Game 3.
Actually, the teams have been comparatively sedate in 2026. As for their fans on social media … ah, we’ll leave that alone.
But a Dodgers-Padres postseason series would almost certainly bring all of the emotions to the surface. Remember, the Padres not only knocked the Dodgers off in 2022 but had them on the ropes in 2024, one game away from another early elimination, before an 8-0 victory in a Game 4 bullpen game in San Diego reversed the momentum.
Also, keep in mind that after the Padres had knocked out Clayton Kershaw in an early season game in San Diego in 2023, a “Crying Kershaw” meme was posted on the Petco Park scoreboard. Consider, too, that the Dodgers gave fans replica Kershaw World Series rings before the first game of this series.
Coincidence? I think not.
And so here we are again. Los Angeles and San Diego split the first two games of their series this week, and while it might not be a major topic of conversation in either clubhouse this week you can bet these teams are casting wary eyes at each other, aware that fate could throw them together in yet another best-of-five (or maybe even best-of-seven) classic.
First things first. After Wednesday night’s game the Dodgers were still one victory or one Atlanta defeat away from clinching the No. 2 spot among division winners and the right to skip the best-of-three Wild Card round. The Padres’ magic number for clinching a wild card berth, likewise, was one.
Will Smith wasn’t about to look ahead. “We’re still approaching it as trying to win some ballgames,” he said. “I don’t think we’ve clinched the bye yet, so we’re still trying to do that.”
But Roberts acknowledged that it was in the back of his mind.
“Yeah, yeah, it’s in there,” he said.
“We’re pretty familiar with these guys. But yeah, absolutely. You know, we’re gathering information on Robbie Ray (Wednesday night’s starter), and, you know, there are guys in the ’pen and (Michael) King (Monday) and we’ll see (Nick) Pivetta (Thursday). So, certainly.”
And, Roberts noted before Wednesday night’s game in response to a question from San Diego Union-Tribune columnist Tom Krasovic, “They’re a thorn in our side and great competition.”
The feeling, I’m sure, is mutual. And while it might wear both teams out, don’t you wish these teams went back to facing each other 18 times during the regular season instead of 13, as they did this season?
Come to think of it, a five-game playoff series … nah, let’s not get too far ahead of ourselves.
jalexander@scng.com

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Dodgers' weak effort vs. Padres in first game without Josue De Paula was frustratingly ironic
item.dc:creator: Katrina Stebbins
item.description: On Wednesday, the Los Angeles Dodgers reactived Shohei Ohtani from the 15-day IL and optioned Josue De Paula, which was just about the most unpopular decision they could've made. item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday, the Los Angeles Dodgers reactived Shohei Ohtani from the 15-day IL and optioned Josue De Paula, which was just about the most unpopular decision they could've made.
No one can really complain about having Ohtani back, but De Paula had captured the hearts and attentions of Dodgers fans so quickly that we would've preferred the team make a more drastic measure, like cutting Alex Call, than sending De Paula away for the time being.
There is still a distinct chance that the Dodgers enter a petition with the Commissioner's Office to carry De Paula on their postseason rosters, but fans want every second of the No. 1 prospect they can get.
The Dodgers took the field for the second game of three against the San Diego Padres without their electric rookie, and they certainly played like they'd lost a spark.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto is no stranger to getting little-to-no run support from his team. In the fifth, with the Padres already up 2-0 thanks to a Manny Machado homer, Yamamoto gave up back-to-back singles before a Dustin Harris laid down a bunt. Yamamoto fielded and tried to throw to third to get the lead runner, but it sailed into foul territory, allowing a run to score.
The Dodgers offense, meanwhile, only scored a single run on a Tommy Edman sac fly.
Dodgers clearly already missing their sparkplug after Josue De Paula option, loss to Padres
The Dodgers' loss and an Atlanta Braves win kept LA from clinching the first-round bye that escaped them last year. The Padres' win allowed them to pull away from the rest of the crowded NL Wild Card pack. Going into Wednesday's game, the Padres, Chicago Cubs, and Philadelphia Phillies were all tied with the same 87-70 record. The Phillies also lost, which allowed the Padres to pull away by a game in the standings.
Although the Dodgers clinching is still all but inevitable, fans are getting antsier the further we come down to the wire.
There are still some big questions to be answered when the Dodgers get to October, the De Paula vs. Dalton Rushing debate being one of them. Dave Roberts already admitted that it would be an uphill battle for Rushing, given how well and how immediately De Paula established himself.
The offense's lifeless showing against the Padres on Wednesday might've been an indirect plus in De Paula's column. Look what they turned into without him.

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers news: What Dave Roberts said about Shohei Ohtani's 1st game back from IL appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Los Angeles Dodgers designated hitter Shohei Ohtani returned to the lineup Wednesday after spending two weeks on the injured list.
Ohtani was activated before Los Angeles' 5-1 loss to the San Diego Padres after missing time because of left knee soreness and right biceps discomfort. It was his first game since Sept. 7, and he was inserted into the No. 2 spot against Padres left-hander Robbie Ray.
The 32-year-old finished 1-for-4 with a walk and two strikeouts. His first at-bat ended with a 99 mph single to right field, and he later hit a 384-foot flyout to center. His biggest missed opportunity came in the fourth inning, when he struck out with the bases loaded during the Dodgers' best scoring chance.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Despite the result, manager Dave Roberts came away encouraged by what he saw from Ohtani.
"He looked good. I thought the at-bat quality was good," said Roberts. "There wasn't any chase. I thought he hit the ball hardest in his first at-bat. It's been a while since he's played in a game, but it just felt like he wasn't sped up at all."
In his final games before landing on the IL, Ohtani had appeared physically compromised at the plate, including moments when he shook out his arm and winced. Los Angeles placed him on the injured list on Sept. 9 after trying to manage the lingering issues while keeping him available.
Ohtani had begun his hitting program about a week before Wednesday's return and had recently faced simulated pitching. He had entered his last game before the IL stint batting .277 with 30 home runs, 80 RBIs, 89 runs and 80 walks through 134 games.
Roberts said Ohtani is expected to return to the lineup Thursday for the series finale. The Dodgers are also still evaluating their batting order against left-handed pitching for the postseason. Against right-handers, Roberts said he would likely put Ohtani back in the leadoff spot and move Mookie Betts to No. 2.
Betts had occupied the leadoff role while Ohtani was away and was batting .366 with six homers, 21 RBIs, 13 walks and 18 runs in 18 September games.
Ohtani won't take the mound in the playoffs, making his health at the plate all the more important as October approaches.
Related: Shohei Ohtani, Tarik Skubal set to return to Dodgers

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers exec confirms Shohei Ohtani suspicions as injuries potentially impact playoff impact
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: In hindsight, Andrew Friedman made the Dodgers’ handling of Shohei Ohtani’s injury-plagued season this year sound rather simple. Throughout Ohtani’s return to a full-time two-way role, the team’s president of baseball operations said, the Dodgers checked in with the superstar “on a daily basis, a weekly basis” to monitor how he was feeling as he handled both pitching and hitting duties. That process intensified once Ohtani began battling left knee and right arm injuries in the middle of the seas
item.content:encoded:
In hindsight, Andrew Friedman made the Dodgers’ handling of Shohei Ohtani’s injury-plagued season this year sound rather simple.
Throughout Ohtani’s return to a full-time two-way role, the team’s president of baseball operations said, the Dodgers checked in with the superstar “on a daily basis, a weekly basis” to monitor how he was feeling as he handled both pitching and hitting duties.
That process intensified once Ohtani began battling left knee and right arm injuries in the middle of the season, leading both to the decision to remove Ohtani from the starting rotation in early July –– but also to let him continue playing through his ailments as the team’s everyday DH while attempting to ramp back up with a pitching program, as well.
It all reached a tipping point two weeks ago, when a clearly diminished Ohtani was finally placed on the injured list amid a 6-for-52 batting slump, and had any plans of returning to the mound this season scuttled for good.
And now, continuing such dialogue will be crucial over the rest of the campaign, with Ohtani returning from the IL on Wednesday for a postseason push that he and the team hopes will see the 32-year-old slugger rediscover his typical productivity at the plate.
“The most important thing is how much better he feels,” Friedman said, speaking to reporters before Ohtani’s 1-for-4 performance in a loss to the San Diego Padres. “Now, it’s about continuing that as he takes game-intensity at-bats.”
How Ohtani and the Dodgers reached this point, of course, has been the subject of much speculation and criticism over recent weeks.
From the start of the year, the club’s No. 1 priority was having Ohtani at full strength as a hitter entering the playoffs.
That they failed in that endeavour –– even Friedman acknowledged Wednesday that Ohtani probably isn’t back to 100% physically, though also insisted that “Shohei says he feels back to where he was earlier in the year, which is great” –– will be the source of significant retrospection within the organization.
Especially if a compromised Ohtani prevents the Dodgers from winning a third-consecutive World Series this fall.
“There’s no question [the injuries] affected him,” Friedman said. “I think the fact that he feels as good as he does right now is certainly encouraging. Now it’s about making sure that holds.”
Friedman didn’t assign blame for why Ohtani’s season went so wrong. He didn’t second-guess the team’s decision to let him play with his injuries for as long as they did, nor Ohtani’s insistence on trying to try and push through his physical problems.
Every time the sides met to discuss Ohtani’s usage, Friedman said, “his answer has been whatever it takes to help the team win. It legitimately has been that single time.”
The one dynamic Friedman did emphasize upon reflection, however, was whether Ohtani was honest enough with himself about how much his health had deteriorated.
“He’s not always the best reporter of how he feels,” Friedman said. “Freddie [Freeman is] the same way. Clayton Kershaw. I’ve been around a lot of these guys that feel like their job is to be out there to help the team however they can, and sometimes will downplay some things that are bothering them.”
In a vacuum, that isn’t necessarily a bad thing.
Friedman said he had “respect” for Ohtani’s dedication to post as often as possible. He recognized that, “in his mind, he thought the best way to help the team was to go out and play.”
At this point, though, it’s hard not to wonder whether Ohtani pushed himself too hard –– and that the team wasn’t proactive enough in stopping him from doing so.
“I think in his mind, he just thought that what he was dealing with was more minor,” Friedman said, while cutting Ohtani some slack by noting he never received more significant diagnoses than inflammation in both his knee and arm.
“Again, the communication back and forth has been awesome,” Friedman added. “The fully sharing exactly how he’s feeling, maybe not as awesome.”
It has certainly left the Dodgers in a less-than-awesome spot now, uncertain of exactly what version of Ohtani they will get over a grueling October trek.
This week, Friedman said the Dodgers want to get Ohtani “as many at-bats as we can” so he can build “some rhythm and timing” with his swing. However, he also didn’t commit to Ohtani playing all five of the team’s remaining games, wanting to see how he handles his return to action first (Wednesday’s performance, at least, offered some signs of progress).
It means, in the coming weeks, more daily check-ins will continue between Ohtani and the Dodgers.
At this point, it’s the best they can do to manage his health entering the playoffs.
As for the past?
“He was in a good enough spot to help us win,” Friedman said, “and we agreed with that.”

item.title: [nypost.com] Shohei Ohtani is back — but something doesn’t look right with Dodgers star
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez
item.description: Something’s not right. The Dodgers said so without saying so. When Shohei Ohtani returned from the 15-day injured list, they batted him second. This is no knock on Mookie Betts, who led off instead. Betts is an eight-time All-Star who is hitting .317 over his last 42 games, but Ohtani is, well, Ohtani. Ohtani is the best player in baseball when healthy, or even close to healthy. If the Dodgers believed Ohtani could be that player for them in the postseason, they wouldn’t have moved him out of hi
item.content:encoded:
Something’s not right.
The Dodgers said so without saying so.
When Shohei Ohtani returned from the 15-day injured list, they batted him second.
This is no knock on Mookie Betts, who led off instead. Betts is an eight-time All-Star who is hitting .317 over his last 42 games, but Ohtani is, well, Ohtani.
Ohtani is the best player in baseball when healthy, or even close to healthy. If the Dodgers believed Ohtani could be that player for them in the postseason, they wouldn’t have moved him out of his customary spot in the order, and it wouldn’t have mattered how anyone else on their team was hitting or whether the opposing pitcher was right- and left-handed.
Presumably, the Dodgers had more insights into his injured right arm and left knee than they shared.
Which is why enthusiasm over Ohtani’s performance on Wednesday should be tempered.
Without question, Ohtani looked better in the 5-1 loss to the San Diego Padres than he did the last time he played.
That didn’t mean he was back to playing like himself – or that he will be at any time during the playoffs.
The return of a Most Valuable Player can have transformative effects on a team, especially if that Most Valuable Player is as healthy as the Dodgers claimed Ohtani was after resting for two-plus weeks, but President of Baseball Operations Andrew Friedman and manager Dave Roberts both spent time before the game managing expectations.
Asked which version of Ohtani was coming back to the team, Friedman replied, “I mean, these aren’t things there’s a clear answer to.”
Roberts said he wanted to see Ohtani “being controlled, taking good at-bats.”
By that standard, Ohtani’s first game back was a massive triumph.
In the first inning, Ohtani singled off left-hander Robbie Ray on the kind of low pitch he was physically incapable of reaching two or three weeks earlier because of his knee problem.
Ohtani later drove a high 99-mph fastball to the warning track, prompting Dodgers broadcaster Joe Davis to scream: “That is a majestic fly ball!”
“I think if you look back at the last couple weeks when he was active, he wasn’t getting to that pitch,” Roberts said of the four-seamer upstairs from right-hander Bradgley Rodriguez.
For the most part, Ohtani didn’t swing at pitches outside of the strike zone. He worked two-ball counts in each of his first four plate appearances, and drew a walk in the third inning.
The Dodgers would almost certainly take games like this from Ohtani. Regardless of what he actually was and wasn’t able to do, the Padres viewed him as a threat, and that alone made him a presence in the lineup.
Ohtani has acknowledged he was unlikely to be 100% healthy again this season, but maintaining an aura of danger will require him to not return to where he was physically leading up to his IL stint.
“Shohei says he feels back to where he was earlier in the year, which is great, which is a good start,” Friedman said. “Now, it’s one thing to feel that way for any player coming back from the IL. When you’re coming back, now the question is, as you start to load on real games and that intensity and that workload, it’s making sure that what we’re done keeps guys in position to be at their best.”
Or, in this case, to at least be viewed as a threat.
Roberts previously described Ohtani as “pain-free” but acknowledged he was still dealing with “discomfort you can play through.” The Dodgers have already seen what happens when Ohtani plays too many games with his arm and knee problems, and every game he plays theoretically pushes him closer to the stage at which the pain becomes unbearable.
How close is Ohtani to that point?
Was the usually-aggressive Ohtani as patient as he was in the batter’s box because he wanted to protect his arm by limiting his swings?
Did his warning-track drive not clear the outfield wall because he hit the ball with the end of his bat or because he wasn’t at full strength?
What should be made of the two at-bats in which he struck out? With the bases loaded, two outs and the count full in the fourth inning, Ohtani was late on a 98.5-mph sinker by David Morgan. In the ninth, Ohtani looked as if he had no chance against closer Mason Miller, who struck him out on three pitches.
Ohtani wasn’t made available to answer any of these questions. By the time the clubhouse opened to reporters, Ohtani was gone.

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Josue De Paula Earns Rave Reviews From Dodgers Leadership
item.dc:creator: Nelson Espinal
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers top prospect Josue De Paula is no longer on the active roster after getting sent down to Triple-A, but the major league team had nothing but positive things to say. De Paula played just 11 games with the Dodgers, but he delivered outstanding offensive production and quickly earned the fanbase’s adoration as a young presence at the plate. However, he was demoted as Shohei Ohtani neared activation from the injured list. Fans who bought into what the 21-year-old showed were disa
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers top prospect Josue De Paula is no longer on the active roster after getting sent down to Triple-A, but the major league team had nothing but positive things to say.
De Paula played just 11 games with the Dodgers, but he delivered outstanding offensive production and quickly earned the fanbase’s adoration as a young presence at the plate.
However, he was demoted as Shohei Ohtani neared activation from the injured list. Fans who bought into what the 21-year-old showed were disappointed, but the organization seemed just as reluctant to see him go.
What the Dodgers think of De Paula
After the move was announced, manager Dave Roberts said De Paula, as the team’s default designated hitter, was set to lose at-bats now that Ohtani returned.
Still, De Paula earned a postseason look, and the team will factor him into its plans.
“We had a runway to give him, which we gave him, and he performed more than admirably. He’s a part of the conversation, and he’s earned that, and that’s what I told him last night,” Roberts said to the media, including Dodgers Nation’s Noel Sanchez.
In terms of skill set, Roberts sees all of De Paul’s traits — the plate approach, swing decision, and vision to deliver in the postseason.
“He’s just a special hitter,” Roberts added. “Hitters don’t see the ball that quickly out of hand; it’s a gift. Just the ability to [limit] chase, I think that lines up in the postseason. And no moment is going to be too big for that kid.”
De Paula’s impressive numbers
Through 11 games in the big leagues, De Paul is hitting .323/.500/.545 with a 1.081 OPS. He is getting on base during half of his plate appearances, and he is really making hitters work.
Andrew Friedman, the president of baseball operations, had been following De Paula closely, and despite the otherworldly production, the Dodgers executive was not surprised.
“It’s what you expect, but you never really know until you see it,” Friedman said to the media, including Dodgers Nation.
“But it obviously really stood out, and he’s done everything he can to put himself in a position to be in the conversation for us as we’re making our postseason roster.”
Meanwhile, Josue De Paula gets the chance to show what he can do defensively in Triple-A while the Dodgers decide.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Dodgers' push for first-round bye, favorable playoff schedule means more for Miguel Rojas
